[0:00–0:02] Good morning. Last week we compared the forming packages and spent half an hour on DEFORM. Today we open one window in the DEFORM pre-processor – the Material window – and stay there for two hours. That sounds narrow, but almost every number the simulation gives back – press force, temperature, die fill, grain size, cracks – is computed from what you type into that window. By the end of today you should be able to look at a material in DEFORM and say which data it needs for your process, where those data come from, and when you cannot trust them.

Structure follows DEFORM V14 manual, Chapter 10 “Material Data”

[0:02–0:04] Here is the plan. The order follows the tabs of the Material window and Chapter 10 of the DEFORM manual. The biggest block, half an hour, is flow stress, because for bulk forming it decides most of the answer. Then yield criteria and hardening – important for sheet metal and springback – creep, thermal data and the 'beyond mechanics' data used for microstructure and heat treatment. There is no break, so I will put a short question to you every few slides – please answer, it keeps us both awake.
Why it mattersGarbage in, garbage out

Same part, same mesh, same friction — two flow curves

  • Upsetting Ø20 × 30 mm → 15 mm, μ = 0.1
  • A: library curve “C45, cold”
  • B: own test of the “same” grade (different heat, annealed)
  • End force: 540 kN vs 427 kN — Δ ≈ 27 %
  • Mesh refinement changes the force by a few % — the material data by tens of %
Material data drive: force & energy · temperature · die fill · damage · springback · grain size · hardness

Slab-method estimate with σ = Kεⁿ (computed for this slide)

[0:04–0:10] Let me start with a small numerical experiment. We upset a cylinder 20 millimetres in diameter and 30 high down to 15. Same geometry, same friction coefficient. The only difference is the flow curve. Curve A is a typical library curve for a C45 steel in cold condition; curve B is what you might measure on your own annealed bar of the same nominal grade. The forces at the end of the stroke are about 540 and 427 kilonewtons – a difference of roughly 27 percent. If you refine the mesh you change the force by a few percent. If you choose the wrong flow curve you change it by tens of percent – and you might order the wrong press. This is the meaning of 'garbage in, garbage out'. The solver is very good at solving the equations; it has no idea whether the material you gave it is the material on the shop floor. That is your job, and it is the job of today's lecture. Look at the box at the bottom: force and energy, temperature, die fill, damage, springback, microstructure – every one of these outputs depends on a different part of the material data. We will meet all of them.
Material windowLayout

The DEFORM Material window

Material window, Elastic tab — copper C10100 (DEFORM-3D)

  • Material list — all materials of the project; each object points to one
  • Regular / Mixture — single phase or several phases
  • Phase — Add, Remove, Transformation, Grain
  • Tabs: Plastic · Elastic · Thermal · Diffusion · Dislocation · Hardness · Elec./Mag. · Advanced · Texture
  • Buttons: New, Delete, Load from lib, Save in lib, Import, Export, Copy prop., Unit conv.
  • Each property: Constant or f(Temp), edited in a table (pencil icon)
[0:10–0:13] This is the window. On the left the material list: every material used in the project, and every object – the billet, a die – refers to one of them by number. Top right the switch between Regular and Mixture; under it the Phase buttons that become active for mixtures. Across the middle you see the tabs. Plastic holds the flow stress, yield function and hardening. Elastic – Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio and thermal expansion. Thermal – conductivity, heat capacity, emissivity and density. Then Diffusion, Dislocation, Hardness, Electro-magnetic, Advanced and Texture, which we will touch in block 8. Two practical details. Each value can be a constant or a function of temperature; the pencil icon opens the table. And at the bottom right there is the Unit conversion button – remember it, we need it in three minutes.
Material windowLibrary

Material library: load, save, import, export

Load from lib — choose class (steel, Al, Ti, Ni, Cu, die steels …), grade and temperature range
↓
Material copied into the project (.KEY / .DB) — edits stay local
↓
Save in lib — your own tested data for the next project
↓
Export / Import — material file (.KEY) between users, sites, versions
Library grades carry a validity range in the name, e.g. cold 20 °C or hot 900–1200 °C. A “cold” curve in a hot forging is a silent error.

Multiple operations — heating, forging, trimming: one material, many temperatures (© SFTC)

[0:13–0:15] Most of you will start with the library. Load from library gives you a list by material class, then by grade. The important point: the material is copied into your project. If you edit it, you edit your copy, not the library. When you have measured your own data, use Save in library so the next project starts from your data, not from the generic ones. Export and Import move a material as a file – between colleagues, between the university and a company, or between DEFORM versions. And the warning box: library grades are measured over a certain range of temperature and strain rate, and that range is usually written in the name. If you take a cold-forming curve into a hot forging simulation at 1100 degrees, DEFORM will not complain – it will extrapolate, and the result will be wrong. We come back to extrapolation in block 4.
Material windowRegular vs Mixture

Regular material or Mixture of phases?

RegularMixture
Phasesone2 … n (austenite, ferrite, pearlite, bainite, martensite …)
Dataone set per tabone set per phase + transformation data
Useforming, machiningheat treatment, quenching, carburising
Mixture rule: \( P = \sum_i \xi_i\,P_i, \quad \sum_i \xi_i = 1 \)
  • \(\xi_i\) volume fraction of phase \(i\), \(P_i\) its property (σ̄, k, E …)
  • Transformation button: kinetics (diffusion / martensite), latent heat, volume change, TRIP

Carburised and quenched helical gear — martensite fraction (© SFTC)

[0:15–0:17] The Regular and Mixture switch decides how many sets of data you need. For forming and machining one phase is enough: the material is a Regular material with one flow curve, one conductivity and so on. For heat treatment the material changes during the simulation – austenite becomes ferrite, pearlite, bainite or martensite. Then you define a Mixture: each phase has its own properties and DEFORM averages them with the volume fractions, as in the simple mixture rule. On top of that the Transformation button holds the inter-phase data: the kinetics, the latent heat released, the volume change, and transformation plasticity. The picture shows why this matters: a carburised and quenched gear with the martensite fraction. Without a mixture, you cannot get that picture, nor the distortion and residual stress that come from it.

[0:17–0:20] Now the trap. The screenshot two slides ago shows copper C10100 with a Young's modulus of 16 679. Sixteen thousand megapascals for copper? That would be seven times too soft. The number is in ksi – the material was saved in English units. 16 679 ksi is 115 gigapascals, which is correct for copper. The same for thermal expansion per degree Fahrenheit, and the reference temperature of 68 Fahrenheit, which is 20 Celsius. DEFORM sets the unit system for the whole problem. If you bring an English-unit material into an SI problem, convert it with the Unit conversion button – do not retype numbers by hand. Note the SI units DEFORM uses: stress in megapascals, density in tonnes per cubic millimetre – 7.7 times ten to the minus nine for steel – and heat capacity per volume in newtons per square millimetre per degree. The right table answers the question 'which tabs do I really need?' An isothermal forging needs only the Plastic tab. As soon as temperature changes, Thermal data are needed. Elastic data only when elastic strains matter – springback, residual stress, die stress. Heat treatment needs everything.
Elastic dataWhen needed

When does DEFORM need elastic data?

  • Rigid-plastic object: elastic strain neglected → no E, ν needed (most forging)
  • Elastic object: dies, die inserts, shrink rings → E, ν, α
  • Elasto-plastic object: springback, residual stress, distortion, heat treatment
$$\varepsilon = \varepsilon^{e} + \varepsilon^{p} + \varepsilon^{th} + \varepsilon^{tr}$$

elastic + plastic + thermal + transformation strain

Elastic range: strain recovers fully on unloading

Die stress analysis with elastic dies (© SFTC)

[0:20–0:22] Elastic data are often left at library defaults, so let us be clear about when they matter. For a rigid-plastic billet – the standard object type for forging – DEFORM neglects elastic strain. Young's modulus is simply not used. The plastic strains are hundreds of percent, the elastic ones a fraction of a percent. Elastic data become essential in three cases. First, elastic dies: the die stress picture here, die inserts and shrink rings. Second, elasto-plastic workpieces where we care about what happens at unloading – springback in sheet forming, residual stresses. Third, heat treatment, where the total strain is the sum of elastic, plastic, thermal and transformation parts, and distortion comes from their interplay.
Elastic dataE, ν

Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio

$$\sigma = E\,\varepsilon^{e}, \qquad \nu = -\frac{\varepsilon_{lat}}{\varepsilon_{ax}}, \qquad G=\frac{E}{2(1+\nu)}$$
MaterialE [GPa]ν
Carbon steel200 – 2100.29 – 0.30
Stainless steel (austenitic)193 – 2000.29
Aluminium alloys69 – 720.33
Titanium Ti-6Al-4V110 – 1140.34
Copper115 – 1200.33
WC-Co die insert500 – 6200.22
  • Springback ∝ σ/E: Al springs back ≈ 3× more than steel at equal stress

Young's modulus across materials (typical handbook values)

[0:22–0:25] Hooke's law, Poisson's ratio and the shear modulus – you know these from strength of materials. In DEFORM you enter E and nu; the shear and bulk moduli follow. Look at the bar chart on a logarithmic scale. Forming metals sit in a narrow band between about 45 and 210 gigapascals; carbide die inserts are three times stiffer than steel, which is exactly why they are used where the die must not deflect. One consequence you will see in the sheet metal lecture: springback scales with stress divided by modulus. Aluminium has a third of the modulus of steel, so for the same stress it springs back about three times more. That is why aluminium car panels are a springback problem.
Elastic dataTemperature dependence

E(T) and thermal expansion α(T)

E(T) of carbon steel — EN 1993-1-2 reduction factor kE

α(T) of several steels in DEFORM (course lecture)

$$\varepsilon^{th} = \alpha(T)\,(T - T_{ref}) \qquad \text{DEFORM: “Thermal expansion” + “Reference temp.”}$$
  • E of steel falls to about 1/3 at 600 °C and almost zero above 1000 °C — use f(Temp) for quenching and hot die stress
  • α is the secant value from Tref; austenite expands more than ferrite (≈ 2.2 vs 1.4·10⁻⁵ /K)
[0:25–0:28] Both elastic properties depend on temperature. The left chart is the Eurocode reduction factor for the modulus of carbon steel: at 600 degrees only about a third of the room-temperature value remains, and close to forging temperature almost nothing. If you simulate quenching from 850 degrees with a constant modulus of 210 gigapascals, you will badly overestimate the stresses at the start of cooling. On the right, thermal expansion of several steels as stored in DEFORM. Notice the field 'Reference temperature' in the Elastic tab. DEFORM uses a secant coefficient: the thermal strain is alpha times the difference from the reference temperature. If you copy instantaneous values from a handbook, they are not the same thing – check which one your source gives. And for heat treatment: austenite expands more than ferrite, so in a mixture each phase needs its own alpha – the volume change at transformation is a separate input in the Transformation dialog.
Elastic dataHyperelastic

Hyperelastic materials: rubber pads and seals

  • Large reversible strains (100–500 %), nearly incompressible (ν → 0.5)
  • Stress from a strain-energy function \(W\) instead of E, ν
Neo-Hookean: \( W = C_{10}(\bar I_1 - 3) \)
Mooney–Rivlin: \( W = C_{10}(\bar I_1-3)+C_{01}(\bar I_2-3) \)
Uniaxial: \( \sigma_{nom} = 2C_{10}\,(\lambda - \lambda^{-2}) \),   \(G = 2C_{10}\)
  • Forming use: rubber-pad forming, flexible dies, seals in assemblies
  • Fit C10, C01 from uniaxial + biaxial tests — never from one test only

Neo-Hookean vs linear elastic in tension and compression

[0:28–0:30] The last elastic topic is hyperelasticity – materials like rubber that stretch several hundred percent and still recover. Linear elasticity fails here: look at the chart. Up to a few percent the two curves agree; at larger stretches the neo-Hookean curve departs from the straight line, and in compression it stiffens strongly. Instead of E and nu, a hyperelastic model uses a strain-energy function. Neo-Hookean has one constant, Mooney–Rivlin two. In forming you meet them in rubber-pad forming of aircraft sheet parts, in flexible dies, and when seals are part of an assembly. One rule: fit the constants from at least two deformation modes, because a fit to tension alone can be unstable in compression. That closes the elastic block. Now the heart of the lecture – flow stress.
Flow stressDefinition

Flow stress: \( \bar\sigma = f(\bar\varepsilon,\ \dot{\bar\varepsilon},\ T) \)

Engineering vs true curve

Permanent strain after the yield point

$$\sigma_t = \sigma_e(1+e), \quad \varepsilon = \ln(1+e)$$
  • Flow stress = true stress needed to keep plastic flow going
  • Depends on strain (hardening), strain rate and temperature; also on prior history
  • Rigid-plastic FEM uses only the plastic part — the curve starts at the yield stress
  • Engineering values are valid only up to necking (uniform elongation)
[0:30–0:33] Flow stress is the true stress needed to keep the material flowing plastically at a given strain, strain rate and temperature. This equation – sigma bar as a function of epsilon bar, epsilon bar dot and T – is the one line you should remember from today. Left: engineering and true curves. Tensile machines give force and elongation, which are engineering values. FEM needs true stress and logarithmic strain; the conversion formulas are here, and they are valid only until necking starts. In the middle: loading beyond the yield point leaves permanent strain. A rigid-plastic code like DEFORM uses only the plastic part of the curve – so the flow curve in DEFORM starts at the initial yield stress at zero plastic strain.
Flow stressT and ε̇

Temperature softens, strain rate strengthens

Stress–strain curves vs temperature and strain rate (course lecture)

RegimeT / TmDominant effect
Cold< 0.3Strain hardening, weak rate effect (m ≈ 0–0.05)
Warm0.3 – 0.5Both, recovery starts
Hot> 0.5 – 0.6Rate + T; hardening balanced by recovery / DRX (m ≈ 0.1–0.2)
  • Strain-rate sensitivity \( m = \partial\ln\bar\sigma/\partial\ln\dot{\bar\varepsilon} \)
  • Superplastic alloys: m ≥ 0.3–0.5
  • Adiabatic heating: \( \Delta T \approx \dfrac{\beta\int\bar\sigma\,d\bar\varepsilon}{\rho\,c_p} \), β ≈ 0.9
[0:33–0:35] Two curves from the course textbook: at fixed strain rate, raising the temperature lowers the curve; at fixed temperature, raising the strain rate raises it. How strong each effect is depends on the homologous temperature – temperature divided by the melting point in kelvin. Cold forming, below about 0.3 of the melting point: strain hardening dominates and the rate sensitivity m is close to zero. Hot forming, above about half the melting point: hardening is balanced by recovery and dynamic recrystallisation, the curve flattens and the rate sensitivity rises to 0.1–0.2. Superplastic alloys go beyond 0.3. Do not forget that temperature itself changes during forming: about 90 percent of the plastic work becomes heat. In fast cold forging the billet can heat up by a hundred degrees or more, so even a 'cold' simulation needs thermal data.
Flow stressTesting

Where flow curves come from

Tensile test
ε < 0.2–0.3, ε̇ ≈ 10⁻³–10⁻¹ s⁻¹ (© ZwickRoell)

Compression (upsetting)
ε ≤ 1, friction correction

Gleeble hot compression
up to ≈ 1700 °C, ε̇ to 10² s⁻¹ (© DSI)

▶ video: Introduction to Gleeble Systems

Split Hopkinson bar (SHPB)
ε̇ ≈ 10²–10⁴ s⁻¹

TestStrengthLimitationDEFORM use
TensionStandard, simple stress stateNecking limits strainSheet, cold forming start of curve
Compression / plane strainLarge strains, hotFriction, barrelling → inverse correctionBulk forming, forging
TorsionVery large strains (ε > 5)Gradient through radiusHot rolling, DRX
SHPBHigh ratesSmall strain, adiabaticMachining, impact (J–C)
[0:35–0:39] Where do these curves come from? Four tests. The tensile test is the standard, but necking limits it to strains of 0.2 or 0.3 – useless on its own for forging, where strains reach 2 or 3. Compression – upsetting a cylinder – reaches strains around one. Its weakness is friction: the specimen barrels, the stress is no longer uniaxial and the measured force must be corrected, often by inverse FEM in DEFORM itself. The Gleeble – the photo – is a thermomechanical simulator. It heats the specimen by direct resistance and compresses it at controlled temperature and strain rate; this is how most hot flow curves in libraries are measured. There is a short Gleeble video linked under the picture if you want to see it. For strain rates of thousands per second – machining, impact – we use the split Hopkinson pressure bar, the sketch on the right: a striker hits a bar, the wave passes through a small specimen, and strain gauges give stress and strain rate. The table says what each test is good for. Torsion I add for completeness: it reaches enormous strains and is used for hot rolling and recrystallisation studies.
Flow stressTabular data

Tabular flow stress \( \bar\sigma(\bar\varepsilon, \dot{\bar\varepsilon}, T) \) and interpolation

DEFORM flow-stress table: curves per T and ε̇ (course lecture)

Value at ε̇ = 50 s⁻¹ from the same four table points: 1012 vs 1028 MPa

  • Table = curves for several T × ε̇, each sampled in ε̄ — the most common format in DEFORM libraries
  • Between points DEFORM interpolates; strain rate spans decades → logarithmic interpolation in ε̇ is the physically sensible choice
  • Typical table: 5–8 temperatures, 4–6 strain rates (10⁻² … 10² s⁻¹), strains 0 … 2
[0:39–0:42] The most common form of flow stress in DEFORM is a table: a set of curves, each for one temperature and one strain rate, each sampled at several strains. On the left you see the DEFORM graph and the table behind it. Between the table points the program has to interpolate. Strain rate in forging spans five or six decades, so it matters how. On the right I took four points of that table – strain rates 1, 10, 100 and 1000 – and asked for the value at 50 per second. Linear interpolation gives about 1012 megapascals, logarithmic about 1028. The difference here is modest, but it grows when the table is coarse. Flow stress is roughly linear in the logarithm of strain rate, so logarithmic interpolation is the physically sensible choice. A good table has five to eight temperatures and four to six strain rates covering the process. That last condition is the subject of the next slide.
Flow stressExtrapolation

Outside the table: extrapolation is a guess

Table measured to 10 s⁻¹, used at 10⁴ s⁻¹: flow stress 8.2 % too low

Process windows (solid) vs test windows (dashed) — schematic

Before running: read the post-processor ranges of ε̄, ε̇ and T and compare them with the table limits. DEFORM does not warn when it leaves the table.
[0:42–0:45] What happens outside the table? The program has to guess, either by holding the last value or by extending the last slope. Left chart: the material follows Johnson–Cook, but the table only goes to 10 per second. Used in a machining simulation at ten thousand per second, the clamped table underestimates the flow stress by about 8.2 percent – and that is at room temperature, with a mild rate effect. The right chart is a map you should keep in your head. Horizontal axis: strain rate on a log scale. Vertical: homologous temperature. Dashed boxes are where tests can reach; solid boxes are where processes run. Hot forging overlaps well with Gleeble compression. Machining sits at strain rates only the Hopkinson bar approaches. Service creep is at strain rates a million times slower than any forming test. So the practical rule: after the first run, open the post-processor, check the maximum strain, strain rate and temperature, and compare them with the table. DEFORM will not warn you.
Flow stressPower law

Power law — the cold forming workhorse

DEFORM: $$\bar\sigma = c\,\bar\varepsilon^{\,n}\,\dot{\bar\varepsilon}^{\,m} + y$$
Hollomon: \( \bar\sigma = K\bar\varepsilon^{\,n} \)   Swift: \( \bar\sigma = K(\varepsilon_0+\bar\varepsilon)^{n} \)
  • \(c, n, m, y\) may be f(T) → simple warm forming
  • \(n\) = strain-hardening exponent = uniform strain in tension
  • Pure Hollomon gives σ = 0 at ε = 0 → use \(y\) or Swift ε0
Material (annealed)K [MPa]n
Low-C steel DC04≈ 5300.22 – 0.26
C45 (normalised)≈ 9000.15 – 0.18
Austenitic stainless 304≈ 13000.40 – 0.50
Al 5xxx≈ 4000.25 – 0.30

σ̄ = c ε̄ⁿ for three hardening exponents

▼ Deep dive: 8 slides on hardening laws and the power law — press ↓
[0:45–0:47] Now the equations. The first one in DEFORM's list is the power law: c times strain to the n, times strain rate to the m, plus y. Without the rate term and offset it is Hollomon's law; Swift adds a pre-strain epsilon zero. The exponent n is the strain-hardening exponent. In a tensile test it equals the uniform strain at necking – that is a nice check of your fit. Look at the chart: with n of 0.35 the curve keeps rising; with 0.1 it is almost flat after the first few percent. Stainless steel has n around 0.45, which is why it work-hardens so much in deep drawing. One practical point. Pure Hollomon gives zero stress at zero strain – an infinitely soft material at the start. DEFORM solves that with the y term, or you use Swift. In DEFORM c, n, m and y can each be a function of temperature, which is enough for simple warm forming. (Optional: press the down arrow for an eight-slide deep dive on hardening laws and the power law – separate script. Otherwise continue to the right.)
Power law ↓1 · The family of hardening laws

From Ludwik to Voce: one flow curve, several equations

LawEquationBehaviour at large εTypical use
Ludwik (1909)\( \sigma = \sigma_0 + K\varepsilon^{n} \)unboundedgeneral, with initial yield
Hollomon (1945)\( \sigma = K\varepsilon^{n} \)unbounded, σ(0) = 0sheet n-value, quick estimates
Swift (1952)\( \sigma = K(\varepsilon_0 + \varepsilon)^{n} \)unbounded, σ(0) = Kε₀ⁿsheet forming, prestrained material
Voce (1948)\( \sigma = \sigma_s - (\sigma_s - \sigma_0)\,e^{-\varepsilon/\varepsilon_c} \)saturates at σsAl alloys, large strains
DEFORM power law\( \bar\sigma = c\,\bar\varepsilon^{\,n}\,\dot{\bar\varepsilon}^{\,m} + y \)unboundedcold forging, heading, extrusion
  • All are empirical: they describe the shape of the curve, not the dislocation physics behind it
  • DEFORM's form = Ludwik + rate term: \(y\) plays the role of σ₀; \(c, n, m, y\) can be f(T)
  • Mixed forms (Swift–Voce: \( \sigma = w\,\sigma_{Swift} + (1-w)\,\sigma_{Voce} \)) are used for AHSS sheet
[PL+0:00–0:03] The power law is the simplest flow-stress model in DEFORM, so it is worth knowing where it comes from and what its relatives are. This short sub-presentation covers the family of hardening laws, the meaning of n and m, how to measure them, and the one big trap – extrapolation. Ludwik proposed in 1909 an initial yield stress plus a power of strain. Hollomon in 1945 dropped the initial yield stress – the famous K epsilon to the n, which gives the n-value of sheet metal. Swift in 1952 added a pre-strain epsilon zero, so the stress at zero strain is not zero. Voce in 1948 took a different route: an exponential approach to a saturation stress. The first three grow without limit; Voce saturates. That difference will matter a lot on slide five. DEFORM's power law is Ludwik's form with an added strain-rate term: c times strain to the n times strain rate to the m, plus y. Remember that all of these are empirical fits to the shape of the curve – none of them is derived from dislocation theory.
Power law ↓2 · Meaning of n

Strain-hardening exponent n and necking

Hardening rate: \( \dfrac{d\sigma}{d\varepsilon} = nK\varepsilon^{n-1} = n\,\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon} \)
Considère (max. force, F = σA): \( dF = 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{d\sigma}{d\varepsilon} = \sigma \)
Hollomon ⇒ \( \varepsilon_u = n \),   \( R_m = K\,n^{n}e^{-n} \)
  • n measures how long the material spreads deformation before it localises
  • High n (austenitic stainless ≈ 0.45) → large uniform elongation, strong work hardening in drawing
  • Low n (cold-worked, HSLA ≈ 0.1) → early necking, little extra strength from forming
  • Check of any fit: n ≈ uniform true strain of the tensile test

Considère construction for K = 530 MPa, n = 0.24 (DC04-type steel)

[PL+0:03–0:06] What does n actually mean? Differentiate Hollomon's law: the hardening rate is n times stress over strain. So n tells how strongly the material hardens relative to its current stress. Now the tensile test. The force is stress times the current area. As the specimen stretches, the area falls and the stress rises. The force reaches its maximum – and necking starts – when the hardening rate drops to the stress itself. That is Considère's criterion. Insert Hollomon's law and you get a beautiful result: the uniform true strain equals n. The chart shows it: the red true-stress curve and the blue hardening-rate curve cross exactly at strain 0.24, where the grey engineering curve – force over original area – has its maximum. So n is a measure of how long the material spreads deformation before it localises. Austenitic stainless steel with n around 0.45 stretches a lot and hardens strongly; a cold-worked or high-strength steel with n of 0.1 necks early. And it gives you a free check: the n you fit should be close to the uniform elongation of the tensile test.
Power law ↓3 · Measuring K and n

Determining K and n: the log–log plot

$$\ln\sigma = \ln K + n\,\ln\varepsilon$$
  1. Tensile test → convert to true stress and true plastic strain (subtract σ/E)
  2. Use the uniform range only, e.g. ε = 2 % … Ag (ISO 10275: n-value)
  3. Linear regression of ln σ on ln ε → slope n, intercept ln K
  4. Ludwik / DEFORM form: first fix y (σ₀ = yield), then fit ln(σ − y) vs ln ε
  5. Cold forging: add compression data to ε ≈ 1 (friction-corrected) — tensile data stop at necking

Not a straight line on log–log? The material does not follow a power law (e.g. Lüders plateau, saturation) — choose Voce or a table.

Synthetic tensile points (K = 530, n = 0.24) — regression returns n = 0.237

[PL+0:06–0:09] How do you get K and n? Take the logarithm of Hollomon's law: ln sigma equals ln K plus n ln epsilon – a straight line on a log–log plot. The procedure: convert the tensile test to true stress and true plastic strain – subtract the elastic part. Use only the uniform range, from about two percent strain to the maximum force; ISO 10275 standardises this as the n-value of sheet. Fit a straight line: the slope is n, the stress at strain one is K. On the chart, synthetic points with n = 0.24 give back n = 0.237. For DEFORM's form with the y term, first fix y as the yield stress, then fit the logarithm of sigma minus y. And the important practical point: a tensile test ends at necking, around 20 to 30 percent strain. Cold forging reaches strains of two or three. For bulk forming you need compression tests to a strain of about one, corrected for friction. If the log–log plot is not straight, the material simply does not follow a power law – use Voce or a table.
Power law ↓4 · Strain-rate exponent m

The strain-rate exponent m and the jump test

$$m = \frac{\partial\ln\bar\sigma}{\partial\ln\dot{\bar\varepsilon}}\bigg|_{\varepsilon,T} \approx \frac{\ln(\sigma_2/\sigma_1)}{\ln(\dot\varepsilon_2/\dot\varepsilon_1)}$$
Conditionm×10 in ε̇ gives
Steel, cold (20 °C)0.005 – 0.02+1 … 5 %
Al alloys, cold≈ 0 – 0.01≈ 0 … 2 %
Warm forming (0.3–0.5 Tm)0.03 – 0.1+7 … 26 %
Hot forming0.1 – 0.2+26 … 58 %
Superplastic≥ 0.3 – 0.5×2 … ×3
  • Jump test: change ε̇ by ×10 at constant ε and T → one specimen gives m
  • Positive m stabilises flow (neck strain rate ↑ → stress ↑) — basis of superplasticity
  • Steels at 150–350 °C: dynamic strain ageing → m < 0, serrated flow (“blue brittleness”)

Strain-rate jump test (m = 0.012, cold steel): small but measurable step

[PL+0:09–0:12] The second exponent is m, the strain-rate sensitivity: the slope of log stress against log strain rate. The simplest way to measure it is a jump test: deform at one rate, suddenly increase it ten times, and read the step in stress. The chart shows it for a cold steel with m of 0.012 – about three percent stress increase for a tenfold rate change. The table gives typical values. Cold metals have m close to zero – that is why the strain-rate term is often dropped in cold forging. In warm forming m rises to several percent, hot forming 0.1 to 0.2, and superplastic alloys reach 0.5 – a tenfold faster deformation then needs three times the stress. Physically, positive m stabilises the flow: where a neck starts, the local strain rate rises, the stress needed rises, and the neck is slowed down. That is the secret of superplastic elongations of several hundred percent. One warning for steels between about 150 and 350 degrees: dynamic strain ageing makes m negative and the flow serrated – the classical blue brittleness range. Avoid warm forming of steel there.
Power law ↓5 · The extrapolation trap

Same tensile data, four laws — and a factor of two at ε = 2

All four laws fitted to the same points (ε = 0.02–0.20); scatter < 1 %

  • All four laws fit the tensile range with < 1 % error
  • At ε̄ = 2 (cold forging, heading): Voce 667, Hollomon 714, Swift 1184, Ludwik 1401 MPa
  • Press force and die stress scale with σ̄ → ≈ ± 35 % error in the load, just from the choice of law
  • Voce saturates (Al, Cu at large ε); power laws keep rising (steels with little recovery)
Rule: fit the law to data that cover the strain range of the process — compression or torsion to ε ≈ 1–2. Use tensile-only fits for sheet forming, not for cold forging.
[PL+0:12–0:16] This is the most important slide of the sub-presentation. I generated tensile-test points between 2 and 20 percent strain and fitted all four laws to them by least squares. In the measured range – the blue band – you cannot tell them apart; the errors are below one percent. Now extrapolate to a strain of two, which is normal in cold heading. Voce gives about 667 megapascals, Hollomon 714, Swift 1184 and Ludwik 1401. That is a factor of two between the lowest and the highest – from the same data. Press force and die stresses scale with the flow stress, so the choice of the law alone changes the predicted load by roughly plus or minus thirty-five percent. Which one is right? None of the tensile data can tell you. Physically, Voce's saturation suits aluminium and copper; steels with little recovery keep hardening more like a power law. Hence the rule: fit to data that cover the strain range of the process. For cold forging that means compression or torsion tests to strains of one or two. Tensile-only fits are fine for sheet forming, not for bulk forming.
Power law ↓6 · Temperature dependence

Power law with temperature: c(T), n(T), m(T), y(T)

  • DEFORM lets each constant be a table f(T) → the power law covers warm forming
  • With rising T: c ↓ (softer), n ↓ (recovery limits hardening), m ↑ (rate sensitivity grows)
  • Linear interpolation between the T points — give enough points around phase changes
  • Adiabatic heating in fast cold forging (ΔT 100–300 K) → even a “cold” simulation should be coupled thermal with c(T)
\( \Delta T \approx \dfrac{\beta}{\rho\,c_p}\int\bar\sigma\,d\bar\varepsilon \),   β ≈ 0.9
Tc [MPa]nmregime
20 °C9000.170.01cold
200 °C8500.15≈ 0 (DSA)avoid
500 °C6200.120.04warm
700 °C3300.080.10warm
900 °C1800.050.15hot → use sinh / table

Illustrative trend for a medium-carbon steel — use measured values for real work

[PL+0:16–0:19] A constant c and n describe only one temperature. DEFORM allows each constant – c, n, m and y – to be a table versus temperature, which stretches the power law into warm forming. The trends are always the same: with rising temperature the material becomes softer, so c falls; recovery limits hardening, so n falls; and the strain-rate sensitivity m rises. The table illustrates this for a medium-carbon steel – the numbers show the trend, not data for a specific grade. Note the row at 200 degrees: dynamic strain ageing, m close to zero or negative – avoid that range. Two practical remarks. DEFORM interpolates linearly between the temperature points, so put enough points where properties change quickly. And in fast cold forging the billet heats by one to three hundred degrees from plastic work. So even a 'cold' simulation should be coupled with heat transfer and use c as a function of temperature. Above about 0.6 of the melting point, switch to the sinh law or a table.
Power law ↓7 · Applications

Where the power law is the right choice

ProcessWhy the power law
Cold forging, heading, cold extrusionHardening dominates, m ≈ 0; needs data to ε ≈ 2
Wire and bar drawingAccumulated strain over passes; n sets the drawing limit
Sheet stamping, deep drawingSwift / Hollomon with n and r-value; n → forming limit
Bending, roll formingModerate strains; springback needs E and hardening model too
Warm forgingc(T), n(T), m(T) tables
Keeler–Brazier (low-C steel): \( FLD_0\,[\%] = (23.3 + 14.13\,t)\,\dfrac{n}{0.21} \),   t in mm

Higher n → higher forming limit in plane strain (empirical, low-carbon steels)

[PL+0:19–0:22] Where is the power law the right choice? Wherever strain hardening dominates and temperature and rate effects are small: cold forging, cold heading and cold extrusion – as long as you have data to large strains. Wire and bar drawing, where strain accumulates over many passes. Sheet stamping and deep drawing, where Swift or Hollomon together with the r-value is the standard description. Bending and roll forming. And with temperature tables, warm forging. For sheet metal n has another very practical meaning. The empirical Keeler–Brazier relation for low-carbon steels links the lowest point of the forming limit diagram – the plane-strain limit – to n and the sheet thickness. The chart shows it: a sheet with n of 0.2 and one millimetre thickness can take about 35 percent major strain in plane strain; with n of 0.1 only half of that. That is why press shops ask for the n-value on every coil certificate.
Power law ↓8 · Limits and summary

Limits, summary and questions

Limits

  • Empirical — no physics, so no safe extrapolation in ε, ε̇ or T
  • Unbounded hardening; Hollomon: σ(0) = 0 → use y (DEFORM) or Swift ε₀
  • Rate and T only through m and f(T) tables — not for hot forming or very high rates
  • No Bauschinger effect, no anisotropy — those come from the yield function and hardening rule (block 5)

Summary

  1. Ludwik, Hollomon, Swift, Voce: same data, different large-strain behaviour
  2. n = uniform strain (Considère); m from jump tests
  3. K, n from a log–log fit in the uniform range
  4. Fit to data covering the process strain — or the load can be off by ≈ ± 35 %

Check yourself

  1. Derive εu = n from the Considère criterion. F = σ·A; at maximum force dF = 0 → dσ/dε = σ. With σ = Kεⁿ: nKεⁿ⁻¹ = Kεⁿ → εu = n.
  2. Why does Hollomon need a y-term or Swift's ε₀ in FEM? Hollomon gives σ(0) = 0 (and an infinite initial slope), so undeformed material would flow at zero stress. The y term or Swift's ε₀ gives a finite initial yield stress.
  3. m = 0.15: how much does σ change if ε̇ rises 100×? σ₂/σ₁ = 1000.15 ≈ 2.0 – the flow stress roughly doubles.
  4. Your fit used tensile data to ε = 0.2. Can you use it for cold heading to ε = 2.5? No. That is extrapolation by more than ten times; laws fitted to the same tensile data differ by a factor of two at ε = 2. Use compression or torsion tests to ε ≈ 1–2.
  5. Which law saturates, and for which materials is that realistic? Voce saturates. Realistic for materials with strong dynamic recovery – aluminium and copper – and at elevated temperature; steels with little recovery keep hardening like a power law.

Press ↑ to return to the main lecture, or → to continue with Johnson–Cook.

[PL+0:22–0:25] To finish: the limits. The power law is empirical, so it cannot be extrapolated safely in strain, strain rate or temperature. Hardening is unbounded, and pure Hollomon starts at zero stress – in FEM always use the y term or Swift's pre-strain. Rate and temperature enter only through m and temperature tables, so it is not a model for hot forming or impact. And it says nothing about the Bauschinger effect or anisotropy – those come from the yield function and the hardening rule, which we discuss in block 5. The summary in four points is on the left. Then five questions – for the third one: a hundredfold rate increase with m of 0.15 raises the stress by a factor of about two. Back up to the main lecture, or straight on to Johnson–Cook.
Flow stressJohnson–Cook

Johnson–Cook — high rates, machining, impact

$$\bar\sigma = \underbrace{(A + B\bar\varepsilon^{\,n})}_{\text{hardening}}\underbrace{\left(1 + C\ln\dot\varepsilon^{*}\right)}_{\text{rate}}\underbrace{\left(1 - T^{*m}\right)}_{\text{softening}}$$
\( \dot\varepsilon^* = \dot{\bar\varepsilon}/\dot\varepsilon_0, \quad T^* = \dfrac{T - T_r}{T_m - T_r} \)
AISI 1045ABnCm
Jaspers & Dautzenberg553 MPa601 MPa0.2340.01341.0
  • Three independent factors — easy to fit, no coupling of T and ε̇
  • DEFORM form adds \(\dot\varepsilon^{*\alpha}\) and \((D - E\,T^{*m})\) for more freedom
  • Fails near Tm and for DRX-dominated hot forming

Johnson–Cook, AISI 1045 (Tr = 20 °C, Tm = 1460 °C)

▼ Deep dive: 9 slides on Johnson–Cook — press ↓
[0:47–0:50] Johnson–Cook is the standard model for machining and impact. It is a product of three brackets: hardening, rate and thermal softening. Each bracket has its own constants and they do not interact – which makes fitting easy, and is also its weakness. The constants here are for AISI 1045, published by Jaspers and Dautzenberg from Hopkinson bar tests, and the chart is computed from them. Going from 1 to ten thousand per second raises the curve by about 12 percent; heating to 700 degrees removes roughly half the strength. DEFORM's version in the dropdown list has two extra parameters – a power on the strain rate and a more flexible temperature bracket. The model is excellent for machining, where strain rates are extreme and temperatures moderate. It is poor near the melting point and in hot forging, where recrystallisation couples temperature and strain rate – which the separate brackets cannot represent. (Optional: press the down arrow for a nine-slide deep dive on Johnson–Cook – separate script. Otherwise continue to the right.)
Johnson–Cook ↓1 · Origin

A model built for impact codes

  • G. R. Johnson & W. H. Cook (Honeywell): “A constitutive model and data for metals subjected to large strains, high strain rates and high temperatures”, 7th Int. Symp. on Ballistics, The Hague, 1983
  • Goal: a model simple enough for explicit impact codes (EPIC) with constants obtainable from a few standard tests
  • Tests: torsion (quasi-static to ≈ 400 s⁻¹, large shear strains), static tension, Hopkinson-bar tension at elevated T
  • Validation: Taylor cylinder impact (strains > 2, rates > 10⁵ s⁻¹) — not used for fitting
  • Companion fracture model: Johnson & Cook, Eng. Fract. Mech. 21 (1985) 31
$$\bar\sigma = \big[A + B\bar\varepsilon^{\,n}\big]\big[1 + C\ln\dot\varepsilon^{*}\big]\big[1 - T^{*m}\big]$$
SymbolMeaningFrom test
Ayield stress at ε̇₀, Trquasi-static
B, nstrain hardeningquasi-static
Cstrain-rate sensitivitySHPB / torsion
mthermal softeningtests at T
ε̇₀, Tr, Tmreference rate (often 1 s⁻¹), reference and melting temperaturechosen / handbook
[JC+0:00–0:03] The Johnson–Cook model was published in 1983 by Gordon Johnson and William Cook of Honeywell, at the International Symposium on Ballistics in The Hague. Their aim was practical: a model simple enough to run in explicit impact codes – their own EPIC code – and with constants that can be obtained from a few standard tests. They used torsion tests over a range of strain rates, static tension, and Hopkinson-bar tension tests at elevated temperatures. They then validated the model on Taylor cylinder impact tests with strains above two – tests that were not used in the fitting. Two years later they published the companion fracture model. On the right: the equation and the five constants. A, B and n come from quasi-static tests; C from high-rate tests; m from tests at elevated temperature. Plus three reference values: the reference strain rate, often one per second; the reference temperature; and the melting temperature.
Johnson–Cook ↓2 · The three brackets

Three independent multipliers

Rate factor: linear in ln ε̇* — +12 % per 4 decades for C = 0.0134

Thermal factor: m < 1 softens early, m > 1 late; zero at Tm

  • Hardening [A + Bεⁿ]: Ludwik law — the flow curve at ε̇₀ and Tr
  • Rate [1 + C ln ε̇*]: below ε̇₀ the factor is < 1 (choose ε̇₀ = lowest test rate, or clip ε̇* ≥ 1); constant C → no upturn above ≈ 10³–10⁴ s⁻¹
  • Thermal [1 − T*ᵐ]: T* < 0 below Tr gives an undefined power for non-integer m → codes set T* = 0
[JC+0:03–0:07] Let us look at each bracket on its own. The first is simply Ludwik's hardening law – the flow curve at the reference strain rate and temperature. The second, left chart, is the rate factor. It is linear in the logarithm of strain rate: with C of 0.0134, four decades of strain rate give twelve percent more stress. Two practical details. Below the reference rate the factor is less than one, so choose the reference as your lowest test rate, or let the code clip it. And because C is constant, the model cannot show the steep upturn of flow stress that many metals show above about a thousand to ten thousand per second. The third, right chart, is thermal softening: one minus the homologous temperature to the power m. With m below one the material softens early; with m above one it keeps its strength longer. At the melting point the stress is zero. Below the reference temperature T star becomes negative, and a non-integer power of a negative number is undefined – most codes simply set T star to zero there.
Johnson–Cook ↓3 · Published constants

MaterialA [MPa]B [MPa]nCmTm [K]Source

  • Constants belong to one material condition (heat treatment, hardness) and one fitting range
  • Large scatter between published sets for the same grade — always check σ(ε) at your ε̇ and T before use

[JC+0:07–0:10] Here are constants from the original 1983 paper, plus the AISI 1045 set we used on the main slide. Note the ranges: A from 90 megapascals for annealed copper to almost 800 for hardened 4340 steel; C between 0.006 and 0.06 – so the rate effect is moderate; and m around one, meaning roughly linear softening with temperature. Two warnings. Each set belongs to one material condition – a heat treatment, a hardness – and to the range of the tests it was fitted to. And published sets for the same grade scatter a lot; for AISI 1045 alone you will find several quite different sets in the literature. So before you use any set, plot the flow curves at your strain rate and temperature and compare them with whatever data you have.
Johnson–Cook ↓4 · Calibration

Determining A, B, n, C and m

1 · A: yield stress at ε̇₀ and Tr (quasi-static tension/compression)
2 · B, n: \( \ln(\sigma - A) = \ln B + n\ln\varepsilon \) — log–log fit of the same test
3 · C: at fixed ε, \( \sigma/\sigma_{ref} = 1 + C\ln\dot\varepsilon^* \) → slope (SHPB at 10³–10⁴ s⁻¹)
4 · m: at fixed ε, ε̇: \( \ln(1 - \sigma/\sigma_{ref}) = m\ln T^* \)
5 · Check: correct SHPB curves for adiabatic heating; validate on an independent test (Taylor, cutting force)

Alternative: fit all five constants together by least squares (or inverse FEM of the tests) — better overall error, less transparent

Step 3 with synthetic points (C = 0.0134): regression gives C = 0.0137

[JC+0:10–0:14] The calibration follows the brackets, which is the big advantage of the model. Step one: A is the yield stress in a quasi-static test at room temperature. Step two: subtract A, take logarithms, and the slope of the log–log plot gives n and the intercept B. Step three, the chart: at a fixed strain, divide the stress at each strain rate by the stress at the reference rate and plot it against the logarithm of strain rate. The slope is C. With synthetic quasi-static and Hopkinson-bar points the regression returns 0.0137. Step four: tests at elevated temperature; the logarithm of one minus the stress ratio against the logarithm of T star gives m. Step five, the check: Hopkinson-bar specimens heat up adiabatically, so correct those curves first; then validate on a test you did not use for fitting. The alternative is a global least-squares fit of all five constants, or inverse FEM – smaller overall error, but you lose the transparency.
Johnson–Cook ↓5 · Adiabatic heating

Thermal softening during fast deformation

AISI 1045 at 10⁴ s⁻¹: plastic work heats the material by ≈ 258 K up to ε = 1

$$\rho\,c_p\,\dot T = \beta\,\bar\sigma\,\dot{\bar\varepsilon}, \qquad \beta \approx 0.9 \;(\text{Taylor–Quinney})$$
  • Above ≈ 10–100 s⁻¹ there is no time for heat conduction → adiabatic
  • J–C's thermal bracket then lowers the hardening curve as T rises
  • Hardening and softening compete → flat or falling curve → adiabatic shear bands, chip segmentation
  • In FEM: always a coupled thermo-mechanical run with ρ, cp(T), k(T); never fit J–C to SHPB curves as if they were isothermal
[JC+0:14–0:17] Johnson–Cook only shows its real character when it is coupled with temperature. In fast deformation about ninety percent of the plastic work becomes heat – the Taylor–Quinney coefficient – and above roughly ten to a hundred per second there is no time for the heat to flow away. The deformation is adiabatic. The chart: AISI 1045 at ten thousand per second. The grey curve is isothermal at 20 degrees. The red curve includes the temperature rise from plastic work – about 258 kelvin at a strain of one – and the thermal bracket pulls the curve down. Hardening and softening compete; where softening wins, deformation localises into adiabatic shear bands. That is exactly the mechanism of segmented chips in machining of hardened steels and titanium. Two consequences for practice: run machining and impact simulations as coupled thermo-mechanical analyses with density, specific heat and conductivity; and never fit Johnson–Cook to Hopkinson-bar curves as if they were isothermal.
Johnson–Cook ↓6 · Limits and modified forms

Limitations — and the modified Johnson–Cook models

Known limitations

  • No coupling: rate sensitivity does not depend on T, hardening does not depend on ε̇ or T
  • Constant C → misses the upturn above 10³–10⁴ s⁻¹ (dislocation drag)
  • Accuracy falls at high T; no recovery, recrystallisation or phase change
  • Unbounded hardening (Ludwik) at large strains
  • BCC metals (yield strongly T-dependent) → Zerilli–Armstrong often better

Modified forms

DEFORM: \( \bar\sigma = (A + B\bar\varepsilon^{\,n})(1 + C\ln\dot\varepsilon^*)\,\dot\varepsilon^{*\alpha}\,(D - E\,T^{*m}) \)
Lin et al. 2010: \( \bar\sigma = (A_1 + B_1\varepsilon + B_2\varepsilon^2)(1 + C_1\ln\dot\varepsilon^*)\,e^{(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2\ln\dot\varepsilon^*)(T - T_r)} \)
Quadratic rate term: \( 1 + C_1\ln\dot\varepsilon^* + C_2(\ln\dot\varepsilon^*)^2 \)
  • Each adds coupling or curvature — and constants; the original stays the default in most codes
[JC+0:17–0:20] The weaknesses come from the same structure that makes the model simple. Because the brackets are multiplied, the rate sensitivity is the same at every temperature, and the hardening is the same at every rate and temperature. The constant C cannot reproduce the steep rise of flow stress above about ten thousand per second. Accuracy falls at high temperatures, there is no recovery or recrystallisation, and hardening is unbounded. For BCC metals with a strongly temperature-dependent yield stress, Zerilli–Armstrong is often better. Hence the many modified versions. DEFORM's own form adds a power-law rate term and a more flexible thermal bracket. Lin and co-workers in 2010 proposed a version with a quadratic hardening term and an exponential temperature term whose slope depends on strain rate – that introduces the missing coupling. Others add a quadratic term in the logarithm of strain rate to capture the high-rate upturn. Each modification adds constants; the original form remains the default in most codes.
Johnson–Cook ↓7 · Fracture model

The Johnson–Cook fracture (damage) model

$$\varepsilon_f = \big[D_1 + D_2\,e^{D_3\eta}\big]\big[1 + D_4\ln\dot\varepsilon^*\big]\big[1 + D_5T^*\big]$$
$$D = \sum\frac{\Delta\bar\varepsilon}{\varepsilon_f} \;\ge\; 1 \;\Rightarrow\; \text{fracture (element deletion)}$$
  • \(\eta = \sigma_m/\bar\sigma\) stress triaxiality: shear 0, tension ⅓, notched bars 0.5–1
  • Same structure as the flow model: triaxiality × rate × temperature
  • 4340 steel (J–C 1985): D₁ = 0.05, D₂ = 3.44, D₃ = −2.12, D₄ = 0.002, D₅ = 0.61
  • Calibration: notched round bars (η), torsion (η ≈ 0), SHPB, hot tests
  • Used for chip separation, blanking, ballistic perforation; compare with Cockcroft–Latham (main slide 41)

Failure strain falls steeply with triaxiality (4340 steel, J–C 1985)

[JC+0:20–0:23] Johnson and Cook added a fracture model in 1985 with the same structure. The strain to fracture depends on stress triaxiality – mean stress over effective stress – times a rate bracket and a temperature bracket. Damage accumulates as the sum of strain increments divided by the current failure strain; when it reaches one, the element fails and is usually deleted. The chart, for 4340 steel with the 1985 constants: the failure strain falls steeply as triaxiality rises – from pure shear at zero, through uniaxial tension at one third, to notched bars with high triaxiality. Higher temperature raises the failure strain. The constants come from notched round bars of different notch radii, torsion tests, Hopkinson-bar and hot tests. The model is used for chip separation in machining, blanking and ballistic perforation. Compare it with the normalised Cockcroft–Latham criterion from the main lecture: Cockcroft–Latham has one constant; Johnson–Cook has five, but captures rate and temperature.
Johnson–Cook ↓8 · Applications

Where Johnson–Cook is used

OperationWhy J–CTypical ε̇, T
Machining (turning, milling, drilling) — DEFORM-3D MachiningChip formation, cutting forces, tool temperature; J–C + J–C damage for segmentation10³–10⁶ s⁻¹, up to ≈ 1000 °C
Impact, ballistics, Taylor testOriginal purpose; robust in explicit codes10³–10⁵ s⁻¹, adiabatic
Crash of car structuresRate hardening of steel and Al sheet1–10³ s⁻¹
High-speed forming (electromagnetic, explosive, hammer)Rate + adiabatic heating10²–10⁴ s⁻¹
Blanking, shearing, punchingLocalised shear, damage model10–10³ s⁻¹
Hot forgingNot recommended — use sinh law or tables> 0.6 Tm

Orthogonal cutting: extreme strain rate in the primary shear zone, high temperature at the tool–chip interface

[JC+0:23–0:26] Where is Johnson–Cook used? First and foremost in machining – it is the default flow-stress model in most cutting simulations, including DEFORM-3D Machining. The sketch shows why: in the primary shear zone strains reach one to five at strain rates up to a million per second, and at the tool–chip interface the temperature rises to 800 or 1000 degrees. Combined with the Johnson–Cook damage model it reproduces chip segmentation. Then its original field: impact, ballistics and Taylor tests, where it is robust and cheap in explicit codes. Crash simulation of car body structures, high-speed forming – electromagnetic, explosive and hammer forging – and blanking and punching. And one line where it is not recommended: hot forging above about 0.6 of the melting point. There the sinh law or measured tables are the right tools – recrystallisation is outside Johnson–Cook's world.
Johnson–Cook ↓9 · Tips and summary

Practical tips, summary and questions

Tips for DEFORM

  • Choose the J–C entry in Plastic → Flow stress; set D = 1, E = 1, α = 0 to get the original form
  • Use Tr, Tm in the problem's temperature unit; set ε̇₀ to the reference rate of the published set
  • Run coupled thermal; enter k(T), ρcp(T)
  • Plot σ(ε) at the process ε̇ and T in the material window before running

Summary

  1. Three independent brackets: hardening × rate × softening
  2. Five constants from quasi-static, SHPB and hot tests
  3. Strong with adiabatic heating: shear bands, chips, impact
  4. Weak where T and ε̇ interact: hot forming, very high rates

Check yourself

  1. Which test gives C, and which gives m? C: tests at several strain rates (quasi-static + SHPB) at the reference temperature – slope of σ/σref vs ln ε̇*. m: tests at elevated temperatures at the reference rate – from ln(1 − σ/σref) vs ln T*.
  2. What does the rate bracket do below ε̇₀, and how do you avoid it? ln ε̇* < 0, so the rate factor drops below 1 (and turns negative at very low rates) – the stress is underestimated. Choose ε̇₀ = the lowest test rate, or clip ε̇* ≥ 1.
  3. Why must SHPB curves be corrected before fitting? At high rates ≈ 90 % of the plastic work becomes heat with no time to escape: the specimen heats adiabatically by up to hundreds of K, so the curve is not isothermal. Uncorrected, thermal softening would end up in n, C and m.
  4. Name two physical effects J–C cannot describe. Any two of: coupling of T and ε̇ (rate sensitivity is the same at every T); the steep stress upturn above ≈ 10⁴ s⁻¹; recovery and recrystallisation; saturation of hardening.
  5. How does triaxiality change the J–C failure strain? Failure strain falls as triaxiality rises (εf ∝ D₁ + D₂·eD₃η, D₃ < 0): high in shear (η = 0), lower in uniaxial tension (η = ⅓), lowest in notched bars.

Press ↑ to return to the main lecture, or → to continue with Zerilli–Armstrong.

[JC+0:26–0:29] Some practical tips for DEFORM. Choose the Johnson–Cook entry in the flow-stress list; with D and E equal to one and alpha equal to zero, DEFORM's extended form reduces to the original. Enter the reference and melting temperatures in the unit of your problem and the reference strain rate of the published set. Run coupled with heat transfer, and plot the curves before running. Summary: three independent brackets – hardening, rate, softening; five constants from quasi-static, Hopkinson-bar and hot tests; strong when combined with adiabatic heating – shear bands, chips, impact; weak where temperature and strain rate interact – hot forming and very high rates. Five questions to check yourselves, then back up to the main lecture or straight on to Zerilli–Armstrong – which, as you will see, was created precisely to fix the missing coupling.
Flow stressZerilli–Armstrong

Zerilli–Armstrong — physics of dislocations, BCC vs FCC

BCC: $$\bar\sigma = C_0 + C_1 e^{-C_3T + C_4T\ln\dot\varepsilon} + C_5\,\bar\varepsilon^{\,n}$$
FCC: $$\bar\sigma = C_0 + C_2\,\bar\varepsilon^{1/2}\,e^{-C_3T + C_4T\ln\dot\varepsilon}$$
  • Based on thermally activated dislocation motion; T in kelvin
  • BCC (steels, Ta, Mo): T and ε̇ affect the yield stress (Peierls barrier)
  • FCC (Cu, Al, Ni, austenite): T and ε̇ affect the hardening
  • DEFORM list: \(\bar\sigma = a + c_1\exp(-c_3T + c_4T\ln\dot{\bar\varepsilon}) + c_5\bar\varepsilon^{\,n}\)

Zerilli–Armstrong (1987) constants for Armco iron and OFHC copper

▼ Deep dive: 10 slides on Zerilli–Armstrong — press ↓
[0:50–0:52] Zerilli and Armstrong derived their model from dislocation mechanics. The key physical insight is the difference between crystal lattices. In body-centred cubic metals – ferritic steels – temperature and strain rate act mainly on the yield stress, because dislocations must overcome the lattice resistance. In face-centred cubic metals – copper, aluminium, nickel – they act on the hardening term. The chart uses the original 1987 constants. Between liquid-nitrogen temperature and room temperature iron loses about half of its strength, copper only about a third – and copper's initial yield stress hardly changes at all. That is the well-known low-temperature brittleness of ferritic steels versus the toughness of copper and austenitic steels. DEFORM offers the BCC form in its list. Use ZA rather than Johnson–Cook when you need a physically based temperature–rate coupling, for example for high-rate forming over a wide temperature range. (Optional: press the down arrow for a ten-slide deep dive on this model – separate script. Otherwise continue to the right.)
Zerilli–Armstrong ↓1 · Origin and motivation

Why a dislocation-based model?

  • F. J. Zerilli & R. W. Armstrong, Naval Surface Warfare Center, J. Appl. Phys. 61 (1987) 1816
  • Goal: flow stress for material dynamics codes — impact, penetration, explosive loading
  • Empirical models (Johnson–Cook 1983) treat T and ε̇ as independent factors and use the same form for every metal
  • Experiments showed: in iron the yield stress depends strongly on T and ε̇; in copper mainly the hardening does
  • Idea: derive the form from thermally activated dislocation motion — and let the crystal lattice decide the form
Johnson–CookZerilli–Armstrong
BasisEmpirical fitDislocation mechanics
T–ε̇ couplingNone (product of brackets)Built in: \(e^{-C_3T + C_4T\ln\dot\varepsilon}\)
LatticeSame form for allBCC / FCC / HCP forms
Grain sizeNot explicitHall–Petch term \(k\,d^{-1/2}\)
TemperatureHomologous T*, needs TmAbsolute T [K]
Constants5 (A, B, n, C, m)5–6 (C₀…C₅, n)
[ZA+0:00–0:02] This short sub-presentation goes deeper into one model, the Zerilli–Armstrong model, which I showed you on one slide a moment ago. We go down, slide by slide, and then come back up to the main line of the lecture. The model was published in 1987 by Frank Zerilli and Ronald Armstrong, who worked for the US Naval Surface Warfare Center. Their customers were people simulating impact, armour penetration and explosive loading – very high strain rates, a wide range of temperatures. The Johnson–Cook model had appeared four years earlier and was the standard. But Johnson–Cook is a fit: three independent brackets, the same shape for every metal. Zerilli and Armstrong noticed something experiments had shown for a long time: iron and copper react differently. In iron the yield stress itself depends strongly on temperature and strain rate. In copper the yield stress hardly changes – it is the hardening that changes. So instead of fitting, they derived the equation from how dislocations move, and let the crystal lattice choose the form. The table summarises the difference. Keep in mind the two key words: coupling of temperature and strain rate, and lattice-dependent form.
Zerilli–Armstrong ↓2 · Physical basis

Thermal activation: dislocations jump over barriers

Short-range barriers can be passed with the help of thermal vibration; long-range ones cannot (schematic)

$$\bar\sigma = \underbrace{\sigma_G}_{\text{athermal}} + \underbrace{\sigma_{th}(T,\dot\varepsilon)}_{\text{thermal}} + \underbrace{k\,d^{-1/2}}_{\text{Hall–Petch}}$$
Arrhenius rate of jumps: $$\dot\varepsilon = \dot\varepsilon_0\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{\Delta G}{k_B T}\right)$$
  • \(\Delta G\) = energy the stress must not supply; the rest comes from thermal vibration
  • Higher T → more help from kT → lower σth
  • Higher ε̇ → less time to wait for a fluctuation → higher σth
  • \(\sigma_G\): long-range stress fields, solutes, initial dislocation density
[ZA+0:02–0:05] Here is the physics. A moving dislocation meets two kinds of obstacles. Long-range obstacles – the stress fields of other dislocations, grain boundaries – are wide; thermal vibration of atoms cannot help to pass them. They give the athermal part, sigma G. Short-range obstacles are narrow peaks: in BCC metals the Peierls hills of the lattice itself, in FCC metals the forest dislocations that a moving dislocation must cut through. Here thermal vibration helps. The applied stress lifts the dislocation part of the way, a thermal fluctuation does the rest. The rate of successful jumps follows an Arrhenius law. From it come the two familiar effects. If the temperature rises, thermal fluctuations are stronger, so less stress is needed. If the strain rate rises, the dislocation has less time to wait for a lucky fluctuation, so more stress is needed. And the grain size adds the Hall–Petch term. So the total flow stress is athermal plus thermal plus Hall–Petch. The whole ZA model is about writing the thermal part correctly.
Zerilli–Armstrong ↓3 · Base mathematics

From the Arrhenius law to the ZA equation

① Thermal stress from thermal activation (activation area A)

$$\sigma_{th} = \frac{M\,\Delta G_0}{A\,b}\;e^{-\beta T}, \qquad \beta = \beta_0 - \beta_1\ln\dot\varepsilon$$

② BCC: A independent of strain (Peierls barrier)

$$\bar\sigma = C_0 + C_1\,e^{-C_3T + C_4T\ln\dot\varepsilon} + C_5\,\bar\varepsilon^{\,n}$$

③ FCC: A ∝ ε̄−1/2 (forest density ρ ∝ ε̄)

$$\bar\sigma = C_0 + C_2\,\bar\varepsilon^{1/2}\,e^{-C_3T + C_4T\ln\dot\varepsilon}$$

④ Common athermal term

\( C_0 = \Delta\sigma_G' + k\,d^{-1/2} \)
ConstantPhysical meaningUnit
C₀athermal stress + Hall–PetchMPa
C₁ (BCC)\(M\Delta G_0/(A b)\) — thermal yield amplitudeMPa
C₂ (FCC)thermal hardening amplitudeMPa
C₃ = β₀thermal softeningK⁻¹
C₄ = β₁T–ε̇ couplingK⁻¹
C₅, n (BCC)athermal strain hardeningMPa, –
k, dHall–Petch slope, grain sizeMPa·mm½, mm
  • M Taylor factor, b Burgers vector, ΔG₀ activation energy at 0 K
  • ε̇ in s⁻¹ (normalised by ε̇₀ = 1 s⁻¹); T always in kelvin
[ZA+0:05–0:09] Now the mathematics, in four steps. Step one: from the Arrhenius law Zerilli and Armstrong derived that the thermal stress decays exponentially with temperature, with an exponent beta that itself depends on the logarithm of strain rate. The amplitude contains the Taylor factor M, the activation energy at absolute zero, the Burgers vector b and the activation area A – the area a dislocation sweeps during one activation event. Step two, BCC metals. The obstacle is the lattice itself – the Peierls barrier – and its size does not change with strain. So A is constant, and the thermal term does not depend on strain. Strain hardening appears as a separate, athermal power-law term C5 times strain to the n. This is the BCC form. Step three, FCC metals. The obstacles are forest dislocations. Their density grows linearly with strain, so the spacing – and the activation area – falls with the square root of strain. Put A proportional to strain to the minus one half into step one, and you get the FCC form: square root of strain multiplied by the exponential. Strain and temperature are now coupled in one term. Step four: C0 collects the athermal stress and the Hall–Petch grain-size term. On the right, the meaning and unit of each constant. Remember the last line: temperature in kelvin, strain rate in per second.
Zerilli–Armstrong ↓4 · Crystal structure decides

BCC vs FCC: the same temperatures, different curves

BCC: curves shift in parallel — T acts on the yield stress

FCC: curves fan out — T acts on the hardening

  • BCC (ferritic steels, Fe, Mo, W, Ta, Nb): high T- and ε̇-sensitive yield, low-temperature brittleness
  • FCC (Cu, Al, Ni, austenitic steels): yield nearly independent of T; hardening rate falls with T
  • HCP (Ti, Mg, Zr): both effects → combined BCC + FCC terms (Zerilli & Armstrong, 1990s)
[ZA+0:09–0:12] Here the difference becomes visible. Both charts are computed from the 1987 constants at a strain rate of one thousand per second, for 77, 296 and 600 kelvin. Left, Armco iron, BCC. The three curves are parallel: temperature shifts the whole curve up or down by the same amount, because it acts on the yield stress. At liquid-nitrogen temperature iron is more than twice as strong at yield as at room temperature. Right, OFHC copper, FCC. All curves start at nearly the same yield stress and then fan out: at low temperature copper hardens faster. Temperature acts on the hardening slope, not on the yield point. Practical consequences: ferritic steels become brittle at low temperatures and are strongly rate-sensitive; austenitic steels, copper and aluminium are not. Hexagonal metals like titanium and magnesium show both features, so for them a combined form with both exponential terms was proposed later.
Zerilli–Armstrong ↓5 · Sensitivities

Where the T and ε̇ sensitivity comes from

Iron: thermal part vanishes with T; athermal part stays

Rate effect from 10⁻³ to 10⁴ s⁻¹: Fe ≈ +350 MPa, Cu ≈ +100 MPa (296 K)

Rate sensitivity: \( \dfrac{\partial\bar\sigma}{\partial\ln\dot\varepsilon} = C_4\,T\,\sigma_{th} \)  — grows with T at first, then falls as σth → 0;   T–ε̇ trade-off: \( \Delta T \leftrightarrow \Delta\ln\dot\varepsilon \cdot \dfrac{C_4 T}{C_3 - C_4\ln\dot\varepsilon} \)
[ZA+0:12–0:15] Two views of the sensitivities. Left, iron at 20 percent strain: the grey area is athermal – strain hardening and grain size – and it does not change with temperature. The red area is the thermal part; at room temperature and high rate it is about two-thirds of the total, and it almost disappears above 800 kelvin. Right, the strain-rate effect at 20 percent strain. From 10 to the minus 3 to 10 to the 4 per second, iron gains about 350 megapascals at room temperature, copper only about 100. The derivative at the bottom explains the pattern: rate sensitivity is C4 times T times the thermal stress. At very low temperature T is small; at high temperature the thermal stress is small; in between, the rate sensitivity is largest. Johnson–Cook, with its constant C, cannot show this – which is exactly why ZA describes BCC metals better at high rates.

\( \bar\sigma = a + c_1\exp(-c_3T + c_4T\ln\dot{\bar\varepsilon}) + c_5\,\bar\varepsilon^{\,n} \) — the BCC form

Modified ZA for hot forming (Samantaray et al. 2009)

$$\bar\sigma = (C_1 + C_2\bar\varepsilon^{\,n})\,\exp\{-(C_3 + C_4\bar\varepsilon)T^* + (C_5 + C_6T^*)\ln\dot\varepsilon^*\}$$
  • \(T^* = T - T_{ref}\), \(\dot\varepsilon^* = \dot\varepsilon/\dot\varepsilon_{ref}\) — fitted to Gleeble hot-compression data
  • Used for 9Cr-1Mo, Ti-modified austenitic SS (R ≈ 0.995, AARE ≈ 5 %), Ti alloys, Al alloys, roll steels

[ZA+0:15–0:18] Here are real constants. For OFHC copper the original paper gives C2 of 890 megapascals, C3 of 0.0028 and C4 of 1.15 times ten to the minus four. C0 is about 65 megapascals, made of an athermal 46.5 plus the Hall–Petch term for a grain size of 73 micrometres. For Armco iron C1 is 1033, C3 about 0.007, C4 about 4 times ten to the minus four, and athermal hardening 266 times strain to the 0.29. Tantalum, used for explosively formed projectiles, has a similar BCC set. DEFORM offers the BCC form directly in the flow-stress dropdown – exactly the expression you see here. On the right, the modified ZA model by Samantaray, Mandal and Bhaduri from 2009. It was developed for hot deformation, fitted to Gleeble compression data. It couples strain into the temperature term and temperature into the rate term. It fits hot-working data of steels well – correlation around 0.995 for a titanium-modified austenitic stainless steel – but note that it has lost the dislocation interpretation; it is a semi-empirical fit with a ZA-like structure. The model is available in DEFORM, LS-DYNA, Ansys explicit codes and via user subroutines in Abaqus.
Zerilli–Armstrong ↓7 · Calibration

How to determine the constants (BCC form)

1 · Test matrix: quasi-static (10⁻³–10⁻¹ s⁻¹) + SHPB (10³ s⁻¹) at 3–5 temperatures, 77 K … 0.5 Tm
2 · Athermal part: C₅, n from hardening \(\bar\sigma - \sigma_y\) vs ε̄ (log–log); C₀ from grain size or high-T plateau
3 · Linearise: \( \ln(\bar\sigma - C_0 - C_5\bar\varepsilon^n) = \ln C_1 - (C_3 - C_4\ln\dot\varepsilon)\,T \)
4 · Slopes for each ε̇ → plot slope vs ln ε̇: intercept C₃, slope C₄
5 · Check: AARE, R; simulate a Taylor test or the compression test in FEM (inverse correction for adiabatic heating)

Step 3–4: straight lines per strain rate (iron constants, synthetic test points)

[ZA+0:18–0:21] How do you get the constants? First the test matrix: quasi-static tests and Hopkinson-bar tests at several temperatures – from liquid nitrogen up to about half the melting point. Second, the athermal part: the strain-hardening exponent and C5 come from the hardening increments on a log–log plot; C0 from grain size or from the plateau at high temperature, where the thermal part has gone. Third – the key trick – take the logarithm of what remains. The logarithm of the thermal stress is linear in temperature, with the intercept ln C1 and a slope that depends on strain rate. The chart shows these straight lines for three strain rates, with synthetic test points scattered around them. Fourth, plot the slopes against the logarithm of strain rate: the intercept gives C3, the slope C4. Finally check the fit with an error measure and, ideally, by simulating an independent test. A warning: at Hopkinson-bar rates the specimen heats up adiabatically, so the measured curve is not isothermal – correct for that before fitting.

Where and in which operations ZA is used

OperationWhy ZATypical ε̇, T

Ballistics, penetrators, EFP linersBCC Fe, Ta, W: strong rate effect at high rates10⁴ s⁻¹, adiabatic
