Taylor impact test: final length and mushroom diameter validate the model

[ZA+0:21–0:24] Where is the model used? The first line is how it was validated: the Taylor impact test. A cylinder is fired at a rigid anvil at 100 to 300 metres per second; it shortens and forms a mushroom. One test covers a whole range of strains, strain rates and temperatures, so comparing the final shape with an FEM simulation checks the model at once. Zerilli and Armstrong did exactly this for copper and iron. Then defence applications – ballistic penetrators and explosively formed projectiles made of iron, tantalum or tungsten, all BCC metals with a strong rate effect. For our field, the most relevant are high-speed machining, where studies have compared ZA and Johnson–Cook for chip formation in steels, and high-speed forming – electromagnetic forming, explosive forming, hammer forging of ferritic materials. Also cold heading and crash simulation, where the BCC-versus-FCC difference matters. Finally, hot forging and rolling, but only through the modified ZA, used as a semi-empirical fit of hot compression data.
Zerilli–Armstrong ↓9 · Limits and tips

Limits of ZA and tips for DEFORM

Known limits

  • Valid roughly below 0.5 Tm: no dynamic recovery, recrystallisation, phase change
  • BCC hardening is athermal → over-predicts hardening at high T
  • Above ≈ 10⁴ s⁻¹ dislocation drag (viscous) dominates — not in the model
  • Comparative study (Banerjee 2005, Cu): very good for room-T Taylor tests; over-estimates the T-dependence at high rates; larger errors at 1235 K
  • Original constants come from one material condition — grain size and prior cold work change C₀

Checklist for DEFORM

  • Choose the ZA entry in Plastic → Flow stress; constants a, c₁, c₃, c₄, c₅, n
  • Constants are fitted with T in kelvin and stress in MPa — check against the problem's unit system before typing published values
  • Use a coupled thermal simulation: adiabatic heating at high rates is essential
  • Plot σ̄(ε̄) at 2–3 temperatures and rates in the material window and compare with the test data
  • Hot forming above 0.6 Tm → prefer tabular data or sinh-Arrhenius
[ZA+0:24–0:27] No model is universal. ZA is physically based only below roughly half the melting temperature: there is no dynamic recovery, no recrystallisation, no phase change. In the BCC form the strain hardening is athermal, so at high temperature it over-predicts hardening. And above about ten thousand per second a different mechanism – viscous dislocation drag – takes over. An independent comparison by Banerjee for copper found ZA very good for room-temperature Taylor tests – the simplest accurate option – but it over-estimates the temperature dependence at high rates and gives larger errors near 1200 kelvin. For DEFORM: choose the ZA entry in the flow-stress list and enter the constants. Published constants assume temperature in kelvin and stress in megapascals – check your problem's unit system before you type them in. Run a coupled thermal simulation, because adiabatic heating is a large part of the physics at high rates. Plot the curves in the material window and compare them with the test data. And for hot forming above about 0.6 of the melting point, use tabular data or sinh-Arrhenius instead.
Zerilli–Armstrong ↓10 · Summary

Zerilli–Armstrong in five points

  1. Derived from thermally activated dislocation motion: σ̄ = athermal + thermal + Hall–Petch
  2. Thermal term \(e^{-C_3T + C_4T\ln\dot\varepsilon}\) couples T and ε̇
  3. BCC: T, ε̇ act on yield (A = const) · FCC: on hardening (A ∝ ε̄−½) · HCP: both
  4. Best for high rates below 0.5 Tm: impact, machining, high-speed forming
  5. Modified ZA = semi-empirical fit for hot forming; DEFORM has the BCC form built in

Check yourself

  1. What is the activation area, and how does it differ between BCC and FCC? The area a dislocation sweeps in one thermally activated jump. BCC: the obstacle is the Peierls barrier of the lattice → constant. FCC: the obstacles are forest dislocations → A ∝ ε̄−½, it shrinks with strain.
  2. Which constant couples temperature and strain rate? C₄ – in the term e−C₃T + C₄T ln ε̇.
  3. Why is ZA better than J–C for iron at 10³ s⁻¹ and −50 °C? Iron is BCC: its yield stress depends strongly and jointly on T and ε̇ (Peierls mechanism). ZA couples them through C₄·T; J–C has a constant C and independent brackets, and T* < 0 below the reference temperature.
  4. Why should you not use the original ZA for forging at 1150 °C? At 1150 °C steel is at ≈ 0.8 Tm: diffusion-controlled flow, dynamic recovery and recrystallisation and austenite govern – none of these is in ZA, and the athermal hardening is over-predicted. Use a table, the sinh law or the modified ZA.

Press ↑ to return to the main lecture, or → to continue directly with hot forming models.

[ZA+0:27–0:30] To close the deep dive, five points. The model is derived from thermally activated dislocation motion. Its exponential term couples temperature and strain rate. The lattice decides the form: BCC – the yield stress is sensitive; FCC – the hardening is sensitive; HCP – both. It is the right choice for high strain rates below about half the melting point: impact, machining, high-speed forming. For hot forming there is the modified, semi-empirical version, and DEFORM has the BCC form built in. Four questions to check yourselves – I will reveal them one by one. Then we go back up to the main lecture and continue with the hot forming models.
Flow stressHot forming models

Hot forming: Zener–Hollomon, sinh-Arrhenius, Norton–Hoff

$$Z = \dot{\bar\varepsilon}\,\exp\!\left(\frac{Q}{RT}\right) = A\,[\sinh(\alpha\bar\sigma)]^{n}$$
$$\Rightarrow\; \bar\sigma = \frac{1}{\alpha}\,\mathrm{arsinh}\!\left[\left(\frac{Z}{A}\right)^{1/n}\right]$$
Norton–Hoff: \( \bar\sigma = K\,(\sqrt3)^{m+1}\,\dot{\bar\varepsilon}^{\,m} \),   \(K = K(T, \bar\varepsilon)\)
  • One parameter Z combines T and ε̇ — higher Z ⇒ higher stress, finer grain
  • C–Mn steel: Q ≈ 300–320 kJ/mol; Al alloys ≈ 150–160 kJ/mol
  • DEFORM: sinh form and power form \(\dot{\bar\varepsilon} = A\bar\sigma^{n}e^{-\Delta H/RT}\) in the list

Steady-state flow stress, sinh-Arrhenius (Q = 312 kJ/mol, n = 4.5, α = 0.012 MPa⁻¹)

▼ Deep dive: 10 slides on Zener–Hollomon and the sinh law — press ↓
[0:52–0:55] For hot forming the standard approach combines temperature and strain rate into one parameter – the Zener–Hollomon parameter Z, strain rate times exp of Q over RT. Q is the activation energy for hot deformation: about 300 to 320 kilojoules per mole for carbon–manganese steels, half that for aluminium. The hyperbolic-sine law of Sellars and Tegart relates Z to the flow stress. It behaves like a power law at low stresses and like an exponential at high stresses, which fits hot-working data over many decades. Invert it, and you have stress as a function of Z – the chart. At 1000 degrees and one per second the steady-state stress is about 110 megapascals; going to 900 degrees and ten per second nearly doubles it. Norton–Hoff is the viscoplastic power law used in several European codes – stress proportional to strain rate to the m. In DEFORM's dropdown you find both the sinh form and the power-exponential form with the activation energy written as delta H. (Optional: press the down arrow for a ten-slide deep dive on Zener–Hollomon and the sinh law – separate script. Otherwise continue to the right.)
Zener–Hollomon ↓1 · Origin and idea

Temperature-compensated strain rate

  • C. Zener & J. H. Hollomon, “Effect of strain rate upon plastic flow of steel”, J. Appl. Phys. 15 (1944) 22
  • Observation: raising ε̇ has the same effect on flow stress as lowering T
  • Both enter through one parameter:
$$Z = \dot{\bar\varepsilon}\,\exp\!\left(\frac{Q}{R\,T}\right)\quad[\mathrm{s^{-1}}]$$
  • Q activation energy [J/mol], R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), T absolute [K]
  • Same Z ⇒ same flow stress and similar microstructure (DRX grain size)
  • Example (Q = 312 kJ/mol): 1000 °C, 1 s⁻¹ → Z ≈ 6.3·10¹² s⁻¹; 900 °C, 10 s⁻¹ → 7.8·10¹⁴; 1200 °C, 0.01 s⁻¹ → 1.2·10⁹

Lines of constant Z: a lab test at low ε̇ can stand in for a fast press at higher T (C–Mn steel)

[ZH+0:00–0:03] This deep dive is about the most widely used idea in hot forming: the Zener–Hollomon parameter, and the hyperbolic-sine law built on it. In 1944 Clarence Zener and John Hollomon published a study on the effect of strain rate on the plastic flow of steel. Their key observation: raising the strain rate has the same effect on the flow stress as lowering the temperature. So both can be combined into one variable – the temperature-compensated strain rate Z: strain rate times exp of Q over RT. Z has the unit of a strain rate, and the temperature must be absolute. Look at the numbers for a carbon–manganese steel. At 1000 degrees and one per second, Z is about 6.3 times ten to the twelfth. At 900 degrees and ten per second it is more than a hundred times higher – 7.8 times ten to the fourteenth; at 1200 degrees and 0.01 per second about ten thousand times lower. The chart shows lines of constant Z in the temperature–strain-rate plane. Every point on one line gives the same flow stress and a similar recrystallised grain size. That is very practical: a slow laboratory test at a higher temperature can represent a fast industrial press at a lower temperature.
Zener–Hollomon ↓2 · Physical basis

Why Arrhenius? Hot working as fast high-temperature creep

  • Above ≈ 0.5 Tm plastic flow is controlled by dislocation climb and cross-slip — both need vacancy diffusion
  • Diffusion is thermally activated: \( D = D_0\,e^{-Q_D/RT} \) → strain rate inherits the Arrhenius term
  • Hardening (dislocation multiplication) and softening (dynamic recovery, DRX) balance → steady state
  • Q of hot working ≥ Q of self-diffusion: alloying, solute drag and particles raise the apparent Q
$$\dot{\bar\varepsilon} = f(\bar\sigma)\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{Q}{RT}\right) \;\Longleftrightarrow\; Z = f(\bar\sigma)$$
MaterialApparent Q for hot working [kJ/mol]
Pure Al (self-diffusion ≈ 142)≈ 140 – 160
Al alloys (6xxx, 7xxx)≈ 140 – 200
Mg alloy AZ31≈ 130 – 170
C–Mn and low-alloy steels (30CrMoA: 262)≈ 260 – 320
Austenitic stainless steels≈ 400 – 460
Ti-6Al-4V: β / (α + β) field≈ 246 / 621
Ni-base superalloys≈ 400 – 600

Typical literature ranges; 30CrMoA from Zhang et al. 2020; Ti-6Al-4V from “Hot deformation characteristics of Ti-6Al-4V” (CityU)

[ZH+0:03–0:06] Why should hot deformation follow an Arrhenius law at all? Above about half the melting temperature, dislocations no longer just glide. They climb and cross-slip around obstacles, and climb needs vacancies to diffuse. Diffusion is a thermally activated process with its own Arrhenius term, so the strain rate inherits it. In that sense hot working is high-temperature creep, only a million times faster. At the same time dislocations multiply – hardening – and are removed by dynamic recovery and dynamic recrystallisation – softening. When the two balance, we reach a steady-state stress, and the steady-state stress is a function of Z alone. The table gives typical apparent activation energies. For pure aluminium it is close to the activation energy of self-diffusion, about 142 kilojoules per mole. Alloying, solutes and particles raise the apparent value: 260 to 320 for carbon and low-alloy steels, 400 to 460 for austenitic stainless steels. Titanium alloy Ti-6Al-4V shows about 246 in the beta field but more than 600 in the two-phase field, because the phase balance changes with temperature. A very high apparent Q is a warning that the microstructure itself is changing.
Zener–Hollomon ↓3 · Three stress laws

Power law, exponential law — and the sinh law that joins them

Low stress (ασ < 0.8): \( Z = A_1\,\bar\sigma^{\,n'} \)
High stress (ασ > 1.2): \( Z = A_2\,e^{\beta\bar\sigma} \)
All stresses (Garofalo 1963; Sellars & Tegart 1966): $$Z = A\,[\sinh(\alpha\bar\sigma)]^{n}, \qquad \alpha \approx \beta / n'$$
  • sinh x ≈ x for small x → power law; sinh x ≈ eˣ/2 for large x → exponential
  • Typical: n ≈ 3–6, α ≈ 0.01–0.04 MPa⁻¹ (steels ≈ 0.01, Al alloys larger)
  • Power law = creep (“power-law breakdown” at high Z); exponential = high-rate hot working

Same constants: the sinh law follows the power law at low σ and the exponential at high σ

[ZH+0:06–0:09] Historically, two laws were used. At low stresses – creep conditions – Z is proportional to stress to a power n prime. At high stresses – fast hot working – Z grows exponentially with stress. Each works in its own range and fails in the other; the transition is known in creep literature as power-law breakdown. Garofalo in 1963, and then Sellars and Tegart in 1966 for hot working, proposed the hyperbolic sine. For small arguments sinh x is about x, so the law becomes a power law. For large arguments sinh x is about e to the x over two, so it becomes exponential. The chart shows this with one set of constants: the red sinh curve follows the blue power law at low stress and the orange exponential at high stress, and switches over in the grey band. The constants: n between about 3 and 6, alpha – the stress multiplier – around 0.01 per megapascal for steels and larger for aluminium alloys. Alpha is usually taken as beta divided by n prime, which already tells you how it is measured.
Zener–Hollomon ↓4 · Base mathematics

Inverting the law and what follows from it

Flow stress as a function of Z

$$\bar\sigma = \frac{1}{\alpha}\ln\!\left\{\left(\frac{Z}{A}\right)^{1/n} + \left[\left(\frac{Z}{A}\right)^{2/n} + 1\right]^{1/2}\right\}$$

Strain-rate sensitivity

$$m = \frac{\partial\ln\bar\sigma}{\partial\ln\dot\varepsilon} = \frac{\tanh(\alpha\bar\sigma)}{n\,\alpha\bar\sigma}$$

Temperature sensitivity

$$\frac{\partial\ln\bar\sigma}{\partial T} = -\,m\,\frac{Q}{R\,T^2}$$
  • Example: 1000 °C, 1 s⁻¹ → σ = 110 MPa, ασ = 1.32, m ≈ 0.15; −10 K ≈ +3 % stress

m falls from 1/n (creep) towards zero (high Z)

[ZH+0:09–0:12] The mathematics in three lines. First, the inversion: arsinh written with a logarithm gives the flow stress directly as a function of Z. This is the formula FEM codes evaluate at every integration point. Second, differentiate with respect to the logarithm of strain rate and you get the strain-rate sensitivity m: tanh of alpha sigma divided by n alpha sigma. At low stress it tends to one over n – the creep value, around 0.2. At high stress it falls towards zero. The chart shows this for three values of n. Third, the temperature sensitivity follows from the same derivative multiplied by Q over R T squared. For our steel at 1000 degrees and one per second, alpha sigma is 1.32, m about 0.15, and cooling by only ten kelvin raises the flow stress by about three percent. That is why die chilling of the surface matters so much in hot forging.
Zener–Hollomon ↓5 · Calibration

Determining α, n, Q and A from hot compression tests

1 · Tests: Gleeble compression, 4–6 T × 4 ε̇ (e.g. 900–1200 °C, 0.01–10 s⁻¹); peak or steady-state σ
2 · n′ and β: slope of ln ε̇ vs ln σ (low σ) and ln ε̇ vs σ (high σ) → α = β/n′
3 · n: \( \ln\dot\varepsilon = \ln A - \dfrac{Q}{RT} + n\ln\sinh(\alpha\sigma) \) → slope of ln sinh vs ln ε̇ = 1/n
4 · Q = n R × slope of ln sinh(ασ) vs 1/T (at constant ε̇)
5 · A from the intercept of ln Z vs ln sinh(ασ); check with R and AARE

Example 30CrMoA (Zhang et al. 2020): α = 0.011 MPa⁻¹, n = 4.40, Q = 262 kJ/mol, A = 3.67·10⁹ s⁻¹, R = 0.983

Step 3: parallel lines, one per temperature (synthetic points from the C–Mn constants)

[ZH+0:12–0:16] How are the four constants found? Start with hot compression tests, typically on a Gleeble: four to six temperatures and four strain rates. From each curve take the peak stress, or the steady-state stress. Step two: plot the logarithm of strain rate against the logarithm of stress – the slope gives n prime – and against stress itself – the slope gives beta. Alpha is beta over n prime. Step three: take the logarithm of the sinh law. Plotting ln sinh of alpha sigma against ln strain rate gives straight, parallel lines, one per temperature – the chart. The slope is one over n. Step four: the vertical spacing of those lines comes from temperature. Plot ln sinh against one over T at constant strain rate; the slope times n times R is the activation energy Q. Step five: the intercept gives A. Under the boxes, a published example for 30CrMoA steel: alpha 0.011, n 4.4, Q 262 kilojoules per mole, with a correlation of 0.98. This is the standard recipe – you will find it in hundreds of papers.
Zener–Hollomon ↓6 · Whole flow curves

From one stress value to the whole flow curve

Typical DRX-type curves: peak, then softening to steady state (illustrative, σ_p from the sinh law)

Strain-compensated Arrhenius model

\( \alpha, n, Q, \ln A = f(\bar\varepsilon) \): polynomials of 4th–6th order, fitted at ε = 0.05 … 0.8
  • Constants solved at each strain → smooth polynomial → full curve σ(ε, ε̇, T)
  • Widely used since Lin et al. 2008 (42CrMo); accuracy typically R ≈ 0.98–0.99, AARE ≈ 3–6 %
  • Downside: 20–30 coefficients, no physics in the polynomials, poor outside the fitted strain range

Physics of the curve

  • Peak stress σp and steady state σss both rise with Z
  • Peak strain grows with Z and d₀: \( \varepsilon_p = a\,d_0^{\,h}\,Z^{\,c} \), DRX starts at \( \varepsilon_c \approx 0.8\,\varepsilon_p \)
[ZH+0:16–0:19] The sinh law gives one number – a peak or steady-state stress. FEM needs the whole curve. Two approaches are common. The first is purely mathematical: the strain-compensated Arrhenius model. You repeat the calibration at many strains – say every 0.05 from 0.05 to 0.8 – and fit each constant, alpha, n, Q and ln A, with a polynomial in strain. Lin and co-workers popularised this in 2008 for 42CrMo steel, and it typically fits with three to six percent error. The price: twenty to thirty coefficients with no physical meaning, and nonsense outside the fitted range of strain. The second approach uses physics: the chart shows the typical shape. The curve rises to a peak, dynamic recrystallisation starts at the critical strain, about 0.8 of the peak strain, and the stress falls to a steady state. The higher Z, the higher the peak and the later it comes. These curves are illustrative, but the trends are exactly what DEFORM's microstructure models use.
Zener–Hollomon ↓7 · Microstructure and processing maps

Z controls grain size — and the safe processing window

DRX grain size: \( d_{DRX} = a\,Z^{-m_d} \),   md ≈ 0.1–0.3
Steady-state stress ↔ grain size: \( \sigma_{ss} \propto d_{DRX}^{-k} \), k ≈ 0.7–0.8
  • Same equations sit in DEFORM's Grain data (JMAK, block 8)
  • Finish forging at higher Z (lower T, faster) → finer grain, higher strength

Processing maps (Prasad, dynamic materials model)

Efficiency: \( \eta = \dfrac{2m}{m+1} \)
Instability: \( \xi = \dfrac{\partial\ln[m/(m+1)]}{\partial\ln\dot\varepsilon} + m < 0 \)
  • DRX domains: η ≈ 30–55 % (pure Al: max ≈ 55 %) · instability: shear bands, cracking

DRX grain size falls with Z (illustrative constants for a C–Mn steel)

[ZH+0:19–0:22] Z is not only about stress. It controls the microstructure. The dynamically recrystallised grain size follows a power law in Z with a small negative exponent, typically 0.1 to 0.3. High temperature and slow forming – low Z – give coarse grains; low temperature and fast forming – high Z – give fine grains. That is why the last forging step is often done colder and faster. These equations are the ones in DEFORM's grain data, which we meet again in block 8. Z also underlies processing maps. In Prasad's dynamic materials model the strain-rate sensitivity m – which we just derived from the sinh law – is turned into an efficiency of power dissipation, two m over m plus one. Regions with high efficiency, around 30 to 55 percent, usually correspond to dynamic recrystallisation – a safe window. Where the instability parameter becomes negative, the material tends to form shear bands or cracks. Process engineers use these maps to choose forging temperature and speed.
Zener–Hollomon ↓8 · Related laws and DEFORM

Norton–Hoff, Hensel–Spittel — and how DEFORM takes the data

Norton–Hoff (viscoplastic power law)

\( \bar\sigma = K(T,\bar\varepsilon)\,(\sqrt3)^{m+1}\,\dot{\bar\varepsilon}^{\,m} \) — e.g. FORGE; m ≈ 0.1–0.2 hot

Hensel–Spittel (empirical, many terms)

\( \bar\sigma = A\,e^{m_1T}\,\bar\varepsilon^{\,m_2}\,\dot{\bar\varepsilon}^{\,m_3}\,e^{m_4/\bar\varepsilon}\,(1+\bar\varepsilon)^{m_5T}\,e^{m_7\bar\varepsilon}\,\dot{\bar\varepsilon}^{\,m_8T}\,T^{m_9} \)
  • Common in FORGE, QForm, Simufact libraries — no Z, but the same data source (hot compression)

DEFORM flow-stress list

sinh: \( \dot{\bar\varepsilon} = A\,[\sinh(\alpha\bar\sigma)]^{n}\exp[-\Delta H/(R\,T_{abs})] \)
power: \( \dot{\bar\varepsilon} = A\,\bar\sigma^{\,n}\exp[-\Delta H/(R\,T_{abs})] \)
  • ΔH ≡ Q; DEFORM uses absolute temperature — check the units it expects for ΔH and R in your unit system
  • Alternative: compute σ(ε, ε̇, T) from the law and enter it as a table — easy to check, and strain hardening at small ε can be added
  • Plot the curves in the material window at the process T and ε̇ before running
[ZH+0:22–0:25] Two relatives you will meet in other software. Norton–Hoff is a viscoplastic power law – stress proportional to strain rate to the m, with a consistency K that depends on temperature and strain. It is the basis of FORGE. Hensel–Spittel is a long empirical product of temperature, strain and strain-rate terms – up to nine exponents – used in the libraries of FORGE, QForm and Simufact. It has no Z, but it is fitted to the same hot compression data. In DEFORM the flow-stress list contains the sinh law and the power law exactly as you see on the right, with the activation energy written as delta H and the temperature absolute. Check which units DEFORM expects for delta H and R in your unit system before typing published values. A practical alternative many engineers prefer: evaluate the law in a spreadsheet or Python, and enter the result as a table of flow stress versus strain, strain rate and temperature. You can see the numbers, add strain hardening at small strains, and plot the curves in the material window before running.
Zener–Hollomon ↓9 · Applications

Where Z and the sinh law are used

OperationUse of Z / sinh law
Hot closed-die forgingFlow stress for die fill and load; Z → DRX grain size in the part
Hot rolling, pass schedulesMean flow stress per pass; Z → recrystallisation between passes
Aluminium extrusionSinh law is the classic model (Sheppard & Wright); exit temperature and speed limits
Isothermal / hot-die forging of Ti, Ni alloysLow ε̇, near-creep regime; m from the sinh law
Process design and scale-upEqual Z: transfer Gleeble results to the press
Processing mapsChoose safe T–ε̇ windows (DRX, no shear bands)
Creep of dies and hot toolsSame Arrhenius structure, low-stress (power-law) branch

Hot forging sequence of a disc (© SFTC)

Ring rolling — Z changes along the roll gap (© SFTC)

[ZH+0:25–0:28] Where is all this used? Practically everywhere above half the melting point. In hot closed-die forging the sinh law gives the flow stress for die fill and press load, and Z feeds the grain-size prediction. In hot rolling it gives the mean flow stress of each pass, and Z decides how much the material recrystallises between passes. Aluminium extrusion is the classic application: the sinh model of Sheppard and Wright has been the standard for decades, used to predict exit temperature and the maximum extrusion speed before surface cracking. For isothermal forging of titanium and nickel alloys the strain rates are low, close to the creep regime, and the strain-rate sensitivity from the sinh law matters. And for process design, the equal-Z idea lets us transfer laboratory results to the press, and processing maps help choose a safe window. The pictures show two typical DEFORM applications: a hot disc forging sequence and ring rolling, where temperature and strain rate – and so Z – change continuously along the roll gap.
Zener–Hollomon ↓10 · Limits and summary

Limits, summary and questions

Limits

  • Steady-state (or peak) law — needs strain compensation or a DRX model for the full curve
  • Q, n, α valid only in the tested T–ε̇ window; phase changes (α/γ, α/β) change Q
  • Not for cold or warm forming: below ≈ 0.5 Tm use power law or J–C
  • Adiabatic heating at high ε̇ distorts test curves → correct before fitting

Summary

  1. Z = ε̇·exp(Q/RT): one parameter for T and ε̇ (T in K)
  2. Physics: thermally activated, diffusion-controlled flow
  3. Sinh law joins power and exponential laws; σ = (1/α)·arsinh[(Z/A)1/n]
  4. Z also sets DRX grain size and processing windows

Check yourself

  1. Compute Z for 1100 °C, 5 s⁻¹ and Q = 300 kJ/mol. T = 1373 K, Q/RT = 300 000 / (8.314 · 1373) ≈ 26.3 → Z = 5 · e26.3 ≈ 1.3·10¹² s⁻¹.
  2. Why does the sinh law work at low and at high stresses? sinh x ≈ x for small x → power law (creep range); sinh x ≈ eˣ/2 for large x → exponential law (power-law breakdown). One formula covers both.
  3. Which plot gives n, and which gives Q? n: ln ε̇ vs ln sinh(ασ) at constant T (slope = n). Q: ln sinh(ασ) vs 1/T at constant ε̇ – Q = R · n · slope.
  4. A forging should get a finer grain. Raise or lower Z — and how in practice? Raise Z: lower temperature and / or higher strain rate – a colder, faster last blow. dDRX ∝ Z−(0.1…0.3).
  5. Why is a strain-compensated model risky beyond ε = 0.8? α, n, Q and ln A are polynomials fitted only up to ε = 0.8; outside that range polynomials diverge and give nonsense, while forging strains (flash, corners) easily exceed it.

Press ↑ to return to the main lecture, or → to continue directly.

[ZH+0:28–0:32] Finally, the limits. The sinh law describes a steady-state or peak stress; for the full curve you need strain compensation or a recrystallisation model. The constants are valid only in the tested window, and a phase change – ferrite to austenite, alpha to beta in titanium – changes the activation energy, so do not fit across it. It is not a model for cold or warm forming. And at high strain rates the test specimen heats up, so correct the data before fitting. Summary in four points: Z combines temperature and strain rate in one parameter, with absolute temperature. Its physics is thermally activated, diffusion-controlled flow. The sinh law joins the power and exponential laws, and inverts to a closed-form flow stress. And Z also sets the recrystallised grain size and the safe processing windows. Five questions to finish. For the first one, take out your calculators: about 1.3 times ten to the twelfth. Then we go back up to the main lecture.
Flow stressBeyond equations

Microstructure-based, AI and user-defined flow stress

Flow-stress options in the Plastic tab (course lecture)

OptionIdeaWhen
Dislocation densityσ̄ = σ₀ + αMGb√ρ; ρ evolves with ε, ε̇, TMulti-step hot forging, DRX
Texture / crystal plasticityGrain orientations → anisotropic flowTi, Mg, sheet, earing
DNN predictorNeural network: chemistry → flow curveNo test data, early design
User routineOwn FORTRAN subroutine compiled into the solverResearch models
ConversionEquation → table; test data → fitted modelLibrary building

The Material Suite (SFTC) fits flow stress from compression data, computes TTT diagrams from composition and JMAK constants.

[0:55–0:57] The dropdown list on the left shows that DEFORM offers more than the classical equations. Let me go through the table. A dislocation-density model computes flow stress from the dislocation density, which itself evolves with strain, strain rate and temperature – useful when the material history matters, for example between hits in multi-step hot forging. Texture and crystal plasticity models start from grain orientations; they matter for titanium, magnesium and sheet earing. Since version 13 there is a deep-neural-network predictor that estimates a flow curve from chemical composition – very handy in early design when you have no test data, but treat it as an estimate. And if nothing fits, you can write your own subroutine and compile it into the solver. Finally, the Material Suite, a separate SFTC tool, fits flow stress from compression tests and computes TTT diagrams and JMAK constants.
Flow stressChoosing a model

Match the model to the process

Decision guide used in this course

[0:57–1:00] To close the flow-stress block, a decision guide. Start with the process. Cold forming – power law, because hardening dominates. Warm and hot forging – a measured table, or a sinh-Arrhenius model if you have to extrapolate in temperature. Machining – Johnson–Cook or Zerilli–Armstrong. Long holding at temperature – a creep model, which is our block 6. Sheet forming with springback – anisotropic yield and kinematic hardening, which is block 5. And under everything the red line: whatever model you pick, compare the range of strain, strain rate and temperature it was fitted to with the range your process reaches. That is half an hour of material in one sentence.
Yield & hardeningEffective stress

From the stress tensor to one number: effective stress

Nine stress components on a volume element (course lecture)

$$\boldsymbol\sigma = \begin{bmatrix}\sigma_{xx} & \tau_{xy} & \tau_{xz}\\ \tau_{yx} & \sigma_{yy} & \tau_{yz}\\ \tau_{zx} & \tau_{zy} & \sigma_{zz}\end{bmatrix}, \quad s_{ij} = \sigma_{ij} - \sigma_m\delta_{ij}$$
$$\bar\sigma = \sqrt{\tfrac{3}{2}\,s_{ij}s_{ij}} = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2}\left[(\sigma_1-\sigma_2)^2+(\sigma_2-\sigma_3)^2+(\sigma_3-\sigma_1)^2\right]}$$
  • Hydrostatic part \(\sigma_m\) does not cause yielding of dense metals
  • Flow curve (uniaxial) is compared with \(\bar\sigma\) → yield when \(\bar\sigma = \sigma_f(\bar\varepsilon, \dot{\bar\varepsilon}, T)\)
  • The yield function defines how \(\bar\sigma\) is computed — Plastic tab, “Yield function type”
[1:00–1:03] A flow curve comes from a uniaxial test, but in a forging every point has a full three-dimensional stress state – nine components, six independent. How do we compare them? We condense the tensor into one number, the effective stress, and say the material yields when the effective stress reaches the flow stress. First we remove the hydrostatic part, the mean stress, because pressure alone does not make dense metals yield. What remains is the deviatoric stress. The von Mises effective stress is the square root of three halves of its double contraction – or, in principal stresses, the familiar formula with the three differences. How exactly the effective stress is computed is set by the yield function in the Plastic tab. That is the next three slides.
Yield & hardeningIsotropic yield

von Mises vs Tresca — isotropic yield criteria

Plane-stress yield loci (σ₃ = 0)

Tresca: \( \tau_{max} = \dfrac{\sigma_1-\sigma_3}{2} = \dfrac{\sigma_0}{2} \)
von Mises: \( \bar\sigma = \sigma_0 \)
  • Max. difference: 15.5 % in pure shear (\(k = \sigma_0/\sqrt3\) vs \(\sigma_0/2\))
  • Experiments on most metals lie closer to von Mises
  • von Mises is smooth → convenient for FEM; DEFORM default

Yield function types in DEFORM (course lecture)

[1:03–1:06] The two classical isotropic criteria. Tresca says yielding starts when the maximum shear stress reaches a critical value – the hexagon. Von Mises uses the effective stress from the previous slide – the ellipse. They agree in uniaxial tension and in equibiaxial tension, and differ most in pure shear, by about 15 percent. Experiments on most metals lie closer to von Mises, and because the ellipse is smooth it is much easier for a finite element solver. That is why von Mises is the default in DEFORM and in almost every forming code. On the right, the DEFORM dropdown for the yield function: von Mises, the Hill quadratic forms, and further options. Bulk forming of isotropic billets – stay with von Mises. Sheets with rolling texture – the next slide.
Yield & hardeningAnisotropy

Hill 1948 — orthotropic anisotropy

$$F(\sigma_{yy}-\sigma_{zz})^2 + G(\sigma_{zz}-\sigma_{xx})^2 + H(\sigma_{xx}-\sigma_{yy})^2 + 2L\tau_{yz}^2 + 2M\tau_{zx}^2 + 2N\tau_{xy}^2 = 1$$
  • 6 constants F, G, H, L, M, N; axes = rolling (x), transverse (y), normal (z)
  • F = G = H = 1/(2σ₀²), L = M = N = 3/(2σ₀²) → von Mises
  • DEFORM: enter FGHLMN directly or R-values (next slide)
From R-values (σ₀ in RD): \( \dfrac{H}{G} = r_0,\quad \dfrac{H}{F} = \dfrac{r_0}{r_{90}},\quad \dfrac{N}{G} = \left(r_{45}+\tfrac12\right)\left(1+\dfrac{r_0}{r_{90}}\right) \)

Hill quadratic (FGHLMN) dialog in DEFORM (course lecture)

[1:06–1:09] Rolled sheets are not isotropic: rolling creates a texture, and the sheet behaves differently along the rolling direction, across it and through the thickness. Hill proposed in 1948 the simplest extension of von Mises for such orthotropic materials – a quadratic function with six constants, F, G, H for the normal stress differences and L, M, N for shear. If you set F, G and H equal and L, M, N three times larger, you get von Mises back – a good check of the input. In DEFORM you can type the six constants directly – this dialog – or let DEFORM compute them from R-values. The relations are at the bottom: three R-values measured at 0, 45 and 90 degrees define the ratios.
Yield & hardeningR-values · Barlat

Lankford R-values, earing and Barlat 91

$$r = \frac{\varepsilon_w}{\varepsilon_t}, \quad \bar r = \frac{r_0 + 2r_{45} + r_{90}}{4}, \quad \Delta r = \frac{r_0 + r_{90} - 2r_{45}}{2}$$
  • High \(\bar r\) → good deep-drawability (DC04: r̄ ≈ 1.6–1.9)
  • \(\Delta r \ne 0\) → ears on drawn cups
  • Al alloys: r < 1 → Hill 48 fails (“anomalous” behaviour)
  • Barlat 91: non-quadratic, exponent a = 6 (BCC) / 8 (FCC) — better for Al

Four ears from planar anisotropy

Hill 48 normal anisotropy, plane stress

[1:09–1:12] The R-value, or Lankford coefficient, is measured in a tensile test of sheet: the ratio of width strain to thickness strain. R greater than one means the sheet resists thinning – good for deep drawing. Deep-drawing steels like DC04 have average R values of about 1.6 to 1.9. The variation of R with direction, delta r, produces ears on drawn cups – the sketch in the middle: four ears at 0 and 90 degrees when delta r is positive. On the right, the Hill yield locus for R of 1.8 and 0.6 compared with von Mises. High R stretches the locus along the biaxial direction – the sheet is stronger in equibiaxial stretching. Aluminium alloys, with R below one, show behaviour Hill 48 cannot describe well; Barlat's 1991 non-quadratic criterion with exponent 8 for FCC metals was designed for that.
Yield & hardeningIsotropic hardening

Isotropic hardening — the yield surface expands

Work hardening: reloading needs a higher stress (course lecture)

Isotropic (left) and kinematic (right) hardening in the deviatoric plane

Isotropic: \( f = \bar\sigma(\boldsymbol\sigma) - \sigma_f(\bar\varepsilon^{p}) = 0 \) — surface radius grows with ε̄p
  • Default in DEFORM; exact for monotonic loading (most forging)
[1:12–1:14] Hardening describes how the yield surface changes as plastic strain accumulates. On the left you see the effect: after deformation the material needs a higher stress to deform further. In isotropic hardening the yield surface keeps its centre and grows uniformly – the left circle. The radius is simply the flow stress at the current plastic strain. That is exactly what the flow curve describes, so isotropic hardening needs no extra data. It is the DEFORM default and it is exact as long as loading goes in one direction – which is true for most forging.
Yield & hardeningKinematic hardening

Kinematic hardening — the yield surface translates

Load reversal after 5 % strain: σ₀ = 300 MPa, linear hardening

\( f = \bar\sigma(\boldsymbol\sigma - \boldsymbol\alpha) - \sigma_0 = 0 \)
Prager / Ziegler: \( \dot{\boldsymbol\alpha} = c\,\dot{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}^{p} \)
Armstrong–Frederick: \( \dot{\boldsymbol\alpha} = c\,\dot{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}^{p} - \gamma\,\boldsymbol\alpha\,\dot{\bar\varepsilon}^{p} \)
  • Bauschinger effect: after tension the material yields earlier in compression
  • Matters for bending–unbending over die radii and drawbeads, cyclic loading
  • Mixed hardening: fraction isotropic + fraction kinematic
  • Data: tension–compression or cyclic shear tests

Hardening rule selection (course lecture)

[1:14–1:17] Kinematic hardening is the other extreme: the yield surface keeps its size but moves, the centre shifted by the back stress alpha. Why would that matter? Look at the chart. We pull the material to 5 percent strain, then reverse. With isotropic hardening it yields again in compression only at the same magnitude it reached in tension. With kinematic hardening the elastic range stays two times sigma zero wide, so it yields in compression much earlier. That early reverse yielding is the Bauschinger effect, and real metals show it. In sheet forming the metal bends and unbends over die radii and drawbeads – exactly a load reversal. Ignore the Bauschinger effect and springback predictions are off. The simplest laws are Prager and Ziegler; Armstrong–Frederick adds saturation. In practice a mixed rule – part isotropic, part kinematic – is selected in the hardening rule dropdown.
Yield & hardeningYoshida–Uemori

Yoshida–Uemori two-surface model and springback

  • Two surfaces: inner yield surface moves inside a bounding surface
  • Captures: early re-yielding, transient Bauschinger, permanent softening, work-hardening stagnation
  • Plus E-modulus degradation with plastic strain: \( E = E_0 - (E_0 - E_a)\,[1 - e^{-\xi\bar\varepsilon^p}] \)
  • 7 material constants (Y, C, B, Rsat, b, m, h) from cyclic tension–compression tests
  • Standard for AHSS springback (DP, TRIP, CP steels)
Springback check list: elasto-plastic object · E(ε̄p) · kinematic / Y-U hardening · anisotropic yield · ≥ 5 elements through thickness

Multi-stage drawing of a casing — unloading after each stage (© SFTC)

[1:17–1:20] Advanced high-strength steels are the toughest springback case, and the model most used for them is Yoshida–Uemori. It uses two surfaces: a small yield surface moving inside a larger bounding surface. That captures details plain kinematic hardening misses – the smooth transient after reversal, permanent softening and hardening stagnation. Another effect matters as much: the unloading modulus of steel drops by 10 to 20 percent after plastic straining. The formula here describes that degradation, and many springback studies show it is as important as the hardening model. Use the box as your springback checklist: elasto-plastic object, degraded modulus, kinematic or Yoshida–Uemori hardening, anisotropic yield and enough elements through the thickness. Yoshida–Uemori needs about seven constants from cyclic tests – not something you find in a generic library.
CreepBasics

Creep: plastic flow at constant stress over time

Creep curves for three stress levels (schematic, computed)

Stages I, II, III (course lecture)

Creep option in the Plastic tab (course lecture)

  • Significant above ≈ 0.4 Tm; strain grows at constant load — I primary, II steady (minimum rate), III tertiary → rupture
  • In DEFORM creep is added to the elasto-plastic strain: \( \dot{\boldsymbol\varepsilon} = \dot{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}^{e} + \dot{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}^{p} + \dot{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}^{c} + \dot{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}^{th} \)
[1:20–1:24] Creep is slow plastic flow at constant stress. It becomes important above roughly 0.4 of the melting temperature – for steel that is from about 450 degrees, for aluminium near room temperature for long times, for lead even at room temperature. The creep curve has three stages: primary creep, where the rate decreases as the material hardens; secondary or steady-state creep at a minimum rate, where hardening and recovery balance; and tertiary creep, where voids and necking accelerate it to rupture. Higher stress – the red curve – shortens everything. In DEFORM creep is an additional strain-rate term next to elastic, plastic and thermal strain, switched on in the Plastic tab for elasto-plastic objects – the dialog on the right.
CreepModels

Creep models available in DEFORM

ModelEquationTypical use
Power law (Norton)\( \dot\varepsilon^{c} = A\,\bar\sigma^{n} \)Steady-state creep, relaxation
Bailey–Norton\( \varepsilon^{c} = A\,\bar\sigma^{n}\,t^{m} \) (m < 1)Primary + secondary creep
Perzyna\( \dot\varepsilon^{c} = \gamma\left\langle \dfrac{\bar\sigma}{\sigma_y} - 1\right\rangle^{p} \)Viscoplasticity above yield
Soderberg\( \dot\varepsilon^{c} = A\left[\exp(\bar\sigma/\sigma_0) - 1\right] \)Low-stress creep
Exponential\( \dot\varepsilon^{c} = A\,e^{B\bar\sigma}\,e^{-Q/RT} \)High-stress creep, T-dependent
Tabular\( \dot\varepsilon^{c} = f(\bar\sigma, T, \varepsilon^{c}) \)Measured data
  • Norton exponent n: 3–8 for dislocation creep; ≈ 1 for diffusion creep
  • Fit constants to the stress and temperature range of the process — creep data extrapolate even worse than flow stress

Model list: DEFORM V14 manual, 10 Material Data – Creep

[1:24–1:27] The DEFORM creep options. The most common is Norton's power law: creep rate proportional to stress to the n. It describes steady-state creep and is used for stress relaxation. Bailey–Norton adds time to a power below one, which also captures primary creep. Perzyna is a viscoplastic overstress model: creep rate depends on how far the stress exceeds the yield stress. Soderberg and the exponential law cover low and high stress ranges, and the tabular option takes measured data directly. A note on the Norton exponent: three to eight means dislocation creep; about one means diffusion creep, typical of fine-grained or superplastic materials. And creep data extrapolate even worse than flow stress – fit them to the stress and temperature range you simulate.
CreepApplications

Where creep shows up in forming

Stress relaxation under fixed strain, Norton n = 5 (computed)

  • Stress relaxation: shrink-fit die rings and bolts at temperature lose preload
  • Isothermal / hot-die forging of Ti and Ni alloys at low ε̇ (10⁻³–10⁻² s⁻¹)
  • Superplastic forming of Ti-6Al-4V, Al 5083 (m ≥ 0.5)
  • Hot sizing, stress-relief annealing: residual stress drops during holding
  • Heat treatment: creep during slow cooling and tempering

Dead-weight creep frame (© DoITPoMS, Univ. of Cambridge)

[1:27–1:30] Where do you meet creep in forming? First, stress relaxation. A shrink-fit ring around a hot die insert is assembled with a certain preload; at working temperature the preload drops by creep. The chart shows Norton relaxation: the stress falls fast at first and then slowly – after tens of hours a large part of the preload is gone. Second, isothermal and hot-die forging of titanium and nickel alloys at very low strain rates, and superplastic forming – there the forming process itself is creep-like. Third, stress-relief annealing and hot sizing, where we want creep to remove residual stress. The photo shows the classic dead-weight creep frame – a test that runs for thousands of hours. That is creep. Now thermal data – fifteen minutes.
Thermal dataThermal tab

The Thermal tab

Thermal tab: conductivity, heat capacity / specific heat, emissivity, density (course lecture)

$$\rho c_p\,\frac{\partial T}{\partial t} = \nabla\cdot(k\nabla T) + \beta\,\bar\sigma\,\dot{\bar\varepsilon} + \dot q_{tr} + \dot q_{EM}$$
PropertySI unit in DEFORMControls
Conductivity k(T)N/(s·°C) = W/(m·K)Heat flow inside the part
Heat capacity ρcp(T)N/(mm²·°C)Heating per unit energy
Emissivity ε–Radiation to environment
Density ρt/mm³Mass (hammers), specific-heat option
[1:30–1:33] The Thermal tab has four lines: conductivity, heat capacity – or specific heat, there is a switch – emissivity and density. They enter the heat equation on the slide: heat stored equals heat conducted plus heat generated by plastic work, by phase transformation and by induction. Note the beta times sigma times epsilon-dot term: that is the plastic work converted to heat, with beta around 0.9 – the coupling between mechanics and temperature. The units again: conductivity in newtons per second per degree, which is the same as watts per metre-kelvin, so you can copy handbook values directly. Heat capacity is per volume, in newtons per square millimetre per degree. That one confuses people – two slides from now.
Thermal dataConductivity

Thermal conductivity k(T)

k(T): carbon steel per EN 1993-1-2; austenitic stainless (typical)

Material, 20 °Ck [W/(m·K)]
Copper≈ 390
Aluminium alloys120 – 200
Carbon steel45 – 54
Hot-work tool steel H13≈ 25 – 29
Stainless 304≈ 15
Ti-6Al-4V≈ 7
  • Low k (Ti, Ni, stainless) → chilled skin at die contact, local overheating in shear bands
  • Carbon steel: k halves from 20 °C to 800 °C — always f(Temp) for hot forging
[1:33–1:36] Conductivity decides how fast heat moves inside the part. The chart: carbon steel starts around 54 watts per metre-kelvin and falls to about 27 at 800 degrees; austenitic stainless starts at 15 and rises. Using a room-temperature constant for a hot forging is therefore a factor-of-two error. The table shows the range: copper conducts 50 times better than titanium. Titanium and nickel alloys conduct heat poorly, so the surface touching a cold die chills while the core stays hot – and in fast deformation the heat stays in shear bands. That is why titanium forgings are so sensitive to die temperature and why titanium is hard to machine.
Thermal dataHeat capacity

Heat capacity or specific heat?

cp(T) of carbon steel — EN 1993-1-2 (peak at the α → γ transformation)

$$\underbrace{\rho\,c_p}_{\text{heat capacity}}\;[\mathrm{N/(mm^2\,°C)}] = \rho\,[\mathrm{t/mm^3}]\times\underbrace{c_p}_{\text{specific heat}}\,[\mathrm{mm^2/(s^2\,°C)}]$$
  • Steel at 20 °C: 7850 kg/m³ × 440 J/(kg·K) ≈ 3.45 N/(mm²·°C)
  • Above 900 °C: cp ≈ 650 J/(kg·K) → ≈ 5.1 N/(mm²·°C)
  • Option Specific heat → DEFORM multiplies by density
  • Latent heat of transformation: in the peak (Regular) or in Transformation data (Mixture) — not both
[1:36–1:39] Here is the confusing one. DEFORM's default is heat capacity – energy per volume per degree – not specific heat per mass. For steel: 7850 kilograms per cubic metre times 440 joules per kilogram-kelvin gives about 3.45 megajoules per cubic metre per kelvin, which in DEFORM units is 3.45 newtons per square millimetre per degree. If you type 440 there, your billet will practically never heat up. The alternative is the Specific heat option; then DEFORM multiplies by density itself – which is the reason density is in the Thermal tab. The chart is the Eurocode specific heat of carbon steel. Notice the peak at about 735 degrees – the alpha to gamma transformation absorbs latent heat. In a Regular material this peak represents the latent heat. In a Mixture the latent heat is entered in the transformation data – so you must not have it twice.
Thermal dataEmissivity · density

Emissivity and density

Radiation + convection at a free surface: $$q = \varepsilon\,\sigma_{SB}\,(T^4 - T_\infty^4) + h_{conv}(T - T_\infty)$$
SurfaceEmissivity ε
Oxidised / scaled steel, hot0.7 – 0.9
Bright machined steel0.2 – 0.4
Polished aluminium0.04 – 0.1
Oxidised titanium0.5 – 0.7
  • At 1200 °C radiation dominates heat loss in transfer from furnace to press
  • Density: mass for hammers and screw presses, specific-heat option, volume change ρ(T) in heat treatment

Open-die cogging of a hot ingot: hours of radiation cooling between passes (© SFTC)

[1:39–1:42] Emissivity controls radiation from free surfaces. Radiation goes with the fourth power of absolute temperature, so for a billet at 1200 degrees it dominates the heat loss during transfer from the furnace to the press. Oxidised steel has an emissivity of 0.7 to 0.9 – the 0.7 you saw in the screenshot. Polished aluminium is below 0.1 – which is why aluminium billets cool slowly by radiation. The picture is open-die cogging of a large ingot: the process takes hours, and most of the temperature loss happens by radiation between the passes. Here emissivity is a first-order input. Density has three roles: mass and inertia for hammers and screw presses, the specific-heat option, and density as a function of temperature, which produces volume change in heat treatment.
Thermal dataInterface HTC

Die–workpiece heat transfer and the Inverse HTC module

1 · Test with thermocouples

2 · Simulated vs measured T(t)

3 · Fitted HTC (© SFTC)

\( q = h\,(T_w - T_d) \),   h = f(pressure, time, lubricant, scale)
  • Not a material property — set in Inter-object, but sits next to k in every heat balance
  • DEFORM defaults: forming contact ≈ 11 N/(s·mm·°C) (= 11 kW/(m²·K)), free surface convection ≈ 0.02
  • Inverse HTC: DEFORM varies h(t) or h(T) until simulated thermocouple curves match the measured ones
  • Same idea used for flow stress: inverse analysis of the compression test
[1:42–1:45] The last thermal item is not in the Material window, but it belongs here: heat transfer between die and workpiece. The heat flux is h times the temperature difference, and h depends on contact pressure, time, lubricant and scale. It is set in the Inter-object dialog. DEFORM's default for forming contact is about 11 kilowatts per square metre-kelvin, and 0.02 for convection at free surfaces. Where do better values come from? The three pictures are SFTC's Inverse HTC module: you run a test with thermocouples in the die or the part, then DEFORM changes h until the simulated temperature curves match the measured ones, and returns the fitted h. Keep this idea of inverse analysis – it is the same trick used to correct friction in compression tests for flow stress. Simulation is not only a user of material data; it is also a tool to measure them.
Beyond mechanicsGrain · JMAK

Recrystallisation and grain size: JMAK (Avrami)

Static recrystallisation, Avrami n = 1.5, t0.5 from 0.1 s to 40 s (illustrative)

$$X = 1 - \exp\!\left[-\beta\left(\frac{t}{t_{0.5}}\right)^{n}\right],\; \beta = \ln 2$$
$$t_{0.5} = a\,d_0^{h}\,\varepsilon^{p}\,\dot\varepsilon^{q}\,e^{Q/RT}$$
DRX grain: \( d_{drx} = a\,d_0^{h}\,\varepsilon^{n}\,\dot\varepsilon^{m}\,e^{Q/RT} \)
  • DRX starts at \(\varepsilon_c \approx 0.8\,\varepsilon_p\)
  • Data: Phase → Grain button

Grain size in a forged Waspaloy disc (© SFTC)

[1:45–1:48] Block 8 – data that go beyond mechanics. First, microstructure. During and after hot deformation the material recrystallises, and the recrystallised fraction follows the JMAK or Avrami equation – the S-shaped curves. The time to 50 percent recrystallisation depends on the initial grain size, strain, strain rate and temperature through an Arrhenius term: at 1100 degrees it is a fraction of a second, at 900 degrees tens of seconds. Similar equations give the grain size after dynamic recrystallisation and grain growth during holding. In DEFORM these constants are entered under the Grain button in the Phase area. The result is the picture on the right: grain size in a forged turbine disc. For aerospace discs the customer specifies grain size, not only shape – so this is a design quantity.
Beyond mechanicsPhases · hardness

Phase transformation kinetics and hardness

Diffusional (ferrite, pearlite, bainite)

\( \xi = 1 - \exp(-b\,t^{n}) \),   b, n from TTT + Scheil additivity

Martensite — Koistinen–Marburger

\( \xi_M = 1 - \exp[-\Omega\,(M_s - T)] \),   Ω ≈ 0.011 K⁻¹

Hardness — Hardness tab

\( HV = \sum_i \xi_i\,HV_i(\text{chem.}, \dot T) \)
  • TTT / CCT from tests or from composition (Material Suite, JMatPro)

Residual hoop stress after quenching a disc (© SFTC)

Cold heading progression — hardness from strain hardening (© SFTC)

[1:48–1:50] For heat treatment, each phase change needs kinetics. Diffusional transformations – ferrite, pearlite, bainite – follow Avrami equations whose constants come from the TTT diagram, extended to continuous cooling by the additivity rule. Martensite is athermal and follows Koistinen–Marburger: the fraction depends only on how far below the Ms temperature you are. Hardness is then a mixture of phase hardnesses, each depending on composition and cooling rate – this is the Hardness tab. TTT data come from dilatometer tests or are computed from composition, for example in SFTC's Material Suite or JMatPro. The pictures: residual hoop stress after quenching a disc – the result of transformation volume change and thermal contraction – and a cold-headed nut, where the hardness distribution comes from strain hardening alone.
Beyond mechanicsDiffusion · EM

Diffusion (carburising) and electro-magnetic data (induction)

Diffusion tab

$$\frac{\partial C}{\partial t} = \nabla\cdot(D\,\nabla C), \quad D = D_0\,e^{-Q/RT}$$
  • Carbon in austenite: D₀ ≈ 2.3·10⁻⁵ m²/s, Q ≈ 148 kJ/mol
  • Surface: carbon potential + mass-transfer coefficient
  • Carbon content → Ms, hardness, TTT shift

Elec./Mag. tab

  • Electrical resistivity ρe(T)
  • Relative magnetic permeability μr(T, H) — drops to 1 above Curie point (≈ 770 °C)
Skin depth: \( \delta = \sqrt{\dfrac{2\rho_e}{\omega\,\mu_0\mu_r}} \)
  • Above Curie: δ grows ≈ 10× → heating zone moves inward

Induction-hardened spur gear (© SFTC)

[1:50–1:52] Two more tabs. Diffusion is used for carburising and nitriding: Fick's second law with a temperature-dependent diffusion coefficient. For carbon in austenite, D zero is about 2.3 times ten to the minus five square metres per second and the activation energy about 148 kilojoules per mole. The carbon content then changes the Ms temperature, the hardness and the TTT curves – so diffusion couples to the phase data. The Electro-magnetic tab holds electrical resistivity and magnetic permeability for induction heating. The key physics is the skin depth. Below the Curie point steel is ferromagnetic and the current flows in a thin skin; above about 770 degrees the permeability drops to one, the skin depth grows roughly tenfold and the heating zone moves inward. Without temperature-dependent permeability you cannot predict the hardened contour on this gear.
Beyond mechanicsFracture

Ductile fracture: normalised Cockcroft–Latham

$$D = \int_0^{\bar\varepsilon_f}\frac{\langle\sigma_1\rangle}{\bar\sigma}\,d\bar\varepsilon \;\ge\; C$$
  • Only tensile max. principal stress counts — compression does no damage
  • C is a material constant, calibrated by simulating a test to its crack strain
  • Typical C: 0.2 – 0.6 (cold steels) — depends on inclusions, T
  • Advanced tab: damage model choice, element deletion threshold
  • Others in DEFORM: Oyane, Rice–Tracey, Brozzo, McClintock, Lemaitre …

Upsetting: tensile hoop stress at the bulge

Cross-wedge rolling — risk of central cavity (Mannesmann effect) (© SFTC)

[1:52–1:55] Last topic: fracture. DEFORM offers many ductile damage criteria; the most used is normalised Cockcroft–Latham. Damage is the integral of the maximum principal stress over effective stress along the strain path, counting only tensile stress. When D reaches the critical value C, a crack is expected. In upsetting – the sketch – the bulging surface has tensile hoop stress, so damage grows there first; that is where cold-heading cracks appear. In cross-wedge rolling, on the right, the centre of the bar is loaded in alternating tension and can open – the Mannesmann effect. The important point for material data: C is not universal. You calibrate it by simulating a test – upsetting, tension, notched bars – to the strain at which the real specimen cracked. Its value depends on the steel cleanliness and temperature. A C value from a different heat of material is only a rough guide.

[1:55–1:58] Here is the summary of the whole lecture in one table – keep it for the seminars. Find your process in the left column and read across which data you need. The bold entries are the ones students most often forget: the thermal set for hot forging, the anisotropy and kinematic hardening for springback, and the transformation data for heat treatment. And the four checks at the bottom, for every simulation: units, validity range, temperature dependence, and one validation against a measurement – the press force or a thermocouple. If all four pass, you can start to trust the colourful pictures.

Quick quiz & sources

  1. Write the general flow-stress function and name its three variables. σ̄ = f(ε̄, ε̇̄, T): effective plastic strain, effective strain rate and temperature.
  2. Why can a rigid-plastic forging simulation run without E and ν? In bulk forming the plastic strains (hundreds of %) dwarf the elastic ones (fractions of a %), so the rigid-plastic formulation neglects elasticity. E and ν are needed only for elastic dies, springback / residual stresses and heat treatment.
  3. Which flow-stress model for machining, which for hot forging — and why? Machining: Johnson–Cook (or Zerilli–Armstrong) – very high strain rates and adiabatic heating. Hot forging: a measured table σ(ε, ε̇, T) or the sinh-Arrhenius law – thermally activated flow where T and ε̇ interact.
  4. What happens if the process exceeds the strain-rate range of a table? DEFORM extrapolates without a warning – it holds the last value or extends the last slope – so the flow stress there is a guess (e.g. a table to 10 s⁻¹ used at 10⁴ s⁻¹ is ≈ 8 % too low). Compare max ε, ε̇, T from the post-processor with the table range.
  5. How do R-values enter the Hill 48 criterion? What does Δr predict? R-values at 0°, 45° and 90° set the ratios of Hill's constants (H/G = r₀, H/F = r₀/r₉₀, …). Δr = (r₀ − 2r₄₅ + r₉₀)/2 predicts earing of drawn cups: Δr > 0 → ears at 0° and 90°, Δr < 0 → ears at 45°.
  6. Isotropic vs kinematic hardening: what happens to the yield surface? Isotropic: the yield surface grows uniformly around a fixed centre (radius = current flow stress). Kinematic: it keeps its size and moves by the back stress α → early reverse yielding (Bauschinger effect), important for springback.
  7. Heat capacity vs specific heat — what does DEFORM expect in SI units? Heat capacity is per volume (ρ·cp), specific heat per mass. DEFORM's default field expects heat capacity: steel ≈ 7850 kg/m³ × 440 J/(kg·K) ≈ 3.45 N/(mm²·°C) = 3.45 MJ/(m³·K). Typing 460 there makes the billet practically never heat up.
  8. How is the Cockcroft–Latham constant C obtained? By calibration: simulate a test (upsetting, tension, notched bar) to the strain at which the real specimen cracked; the damage D at the crack site at that moment is C. It depends on the heat of material, cleanliness and temperature.
